Taylor's New Haven theology of the 'power to the contrary' — an Arminianizing move that licensed the direct, will-targeting revival appeal later systematized by Finney, even as it dissolved the revived churches' doctrinal distinctiveness.
s: Douglas A. Sweeney, Nathaniel Taylor, New Haven Theology, and the Legacy of Jonathan Edwards (OUP, 2003), via DTS Voice and Gale Academic. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: George Whitefield manufactured the sense of a single connected inter-colonial 'awakening' through advance newspaper publicity, serialized self-narrating journals, and a touring body that supplied a single recurring protagonist — so the revival's apparent unity was partly a deliberate communications artifact, not solely spontaneous religious fervor.
s: Frank Lambert, 'Pedlar in Divinity' (Princeton UP, 1994); Harry Stout, The Divine Dramatist (Eerdmans, 1991); Commonplace, 'Reconsidering George Whitefield at 300'. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Whitefield hired the merchant William Seward as a publicist ahead of his first American tour and deployed advance publicity teams to advertise his coming presentations — a technique later copied by Moody, Sunday, and Graham.
s: Frank Lambert, 'Pedlar in Divinity' (Princeton UP, 1994), via Princeton UP and Commonplace. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Charles Finney's 'new measures' (protracted meetings, the anxious bench, public prayer for named persons) and his Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835) codified revival as a reproducible technology — 'not a miracle … a purely philosophical result of the right use of the constituted means' — fusing the New Birth theology, the media instinct, and populism into an operational doctrine.
s: Charles G. Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835), referenced via standard scholarly account; primary text not directly consulted. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: On Finke and Stark's religious-economy model, post-Revolutionary disestablishment created a competitive religious 'free market' in which market-disciplined upstart sects out-recruited subsidized, complacent former establishments, raising overall participation (from under 1-in-5 adherents in 1776 toward ~6-in-10 later).
s: Roger Finke & Rodney Stark, The Churching of America, 1776–2005 (Rutgers UP, rev. 2005). Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Finke and Stark report that between 1776 and 1850 Methodists rose from 2.5% to 34.2% of religious adherents and Baptists from 16.9% to 20.5%, while the formerly established Congregationalists fell from 20.4% to 4.0% and Episcopalians from 15.7% to 3.5% — the pattern the religious-economy model predicts.
s: Finke & Stark figures, via kevinmwatson.com transcription and the Churching of America book page; underlying source is Finke & Stark (Rutgers UP). Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: The religious-economy model's signature prediction — that pluralism raises participation — fails outside the U.S.: Steve Bruce argues diversity undermines rather than promotes religion, and Chaves and Gorski's review concludes the empirical evidence does not support a positive pluralism–participation association in any general sense.
s: Steve Bruce, Choice and Religion (OUP, 1999); Mark Chaves & Philip Gorski, 'Religious Pluralism and Religious Participation,' Annual Review of Sociology (2001), via PMC summary. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Nathan Hatch's mechanism: in the post-1800 Jeffersonian culture primed to reject all credentialed authority, uneducated, charismatic preachers seized religious authority from a learned clergy across five populist movements (Methodists, Baptists, Mormons, Restorationist 'Christians,' the Black church), fueling the upstart surge.
s: Nathan O. Hatch, The Democratization of American Christianity (Yale UP, 1989), via Internet Archive and Google Books. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Paul Johnson reads Rochester's Finney revival (1830–31) as social control: a master-class that had lost paternalistic control over a market-displaced workforce used the revival to internalize labor discipline and temperance in workers, then enforced those norms through economic power over mobility.
s: Paul E. Johnson, A Shopkeeper's Millennium (Hill & Wang, 1978). Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Daniel Walker Howe rejects the 'market revolution' frame — disputing its timing (market change came earlier), its valence (farmers welcomed markets; living standards rose), and its root cause — arguing the truly transformative antebellum force was a 'communications revolution' (telegraph, postal expansion, cheaper printing), which relocates causal weight from commerce back to communications.
s: Daniel Walker Howe, What Hath God Wrought (OUP, 2007), via the Sellers–Howe–Woodward debate (History News Network). Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: The Methodist circuit system (connectionalism) — itinerant circuit riders on fixed loops plus a dense lay infrastructure of class meetings, local preachers, and camp meetings — functioned as a scalable distribution network that reached a dispersed, under-churched frontier population at a cost the settled parish model could not match.
s: John H. Wigger, Taking Heaven by Storm (OUP, 1998), via UI Press and Carwardine review. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: American Methodism grew from fewer than 1,000 members in 1770 to over 250,000 by 1820 — a roughly 250-fold expansion in fifty years — a growth curve plausibly produced only by a scalable distribution technology operating against a dispersing frontier population.
s: John H. Wigger, Taking Heaven by Storm (OUP, 1998). Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: The Cane Ridge, Kentucky, camp meeting of August 1801 drew an estimated 10,000–20,000 people — roughly 10% of Kentucky's population — demonstrating the camp meeting's capacity to aggregate an otherwise unreachable dispersed frontier population at scale.
s: Cane Ridge accounts via Christian History Institute, ExploreKYHistory, WHAS11. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: A transatlantic communication network of correspondence, reprinted accounts, and the first evangelical magazines (1740–48), together with Whitefield's repeated Atlantic crossings, synchronized the American Great Awakening, the English Evangelical Revival, and the Scottish Cambuslang Wark so that participants perceived them as parts of a single God-inspired phenomenon.
s: Susan O'Brien, 'A Transatlantic Community of Saints,' American Historical Review (1986), via abstract/indexing. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: The Great Awakening' is a contested category: Jon Butler called it an 'interpretive fiction' retrofitted by later historians onto discontinuous local revivals, and Frank Lambert argued the revivals were real but their unity was constructed in print as they happened — which makes the communications drivers partly constitutive of, not merely background to, 'the Awakening.
s: Jon Butler, Awash in a Sea of Faith (Harvard UP, 1990); Frank Lambert, Inventing the 'Great Awakening' (Princeton UP, 1999), via Christian Century. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Scholarship on what drove the Second Great Awakening moved through three threads: social control (1960s–80s, e.g. Johnson), Mathews's 'organizing process' hypothesis (1969) as connective tissue, and democratization (1980s–90s, Hatch) — now the default frame — with the current frontier pushing toward communication and 'construction' as the master category.
s: Donald G. Mathews, American Quarterly (1969); three-thread framing via search synthesis (JMU source inaccessible, 403). Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Disestablishment proceeded state by state from Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (enacted 16 January 1786) and the First Amendment's federal bar (1791) to Massachusetts as the last state to disestablish in 1833, creating the non-coerced competitive religious field that the religious-economy driver presupposes.
s: Encyclopedia Virginia, 'Virginia Statute for Establishing Religious Freedom (1786)'; John Witte Jr. & Justin Latterell, 'The Last American Establishment: Massachusetts, 1780–1833' (SSRN). Accessed 202

claims.t: The Asbury University 'Outpouring' began 8 February 2023 in Hughes Auditorium and ran 16 days, drawing an estimated 50,000–70,000 participants (including visitors from Russia and Japan) and spreading globally by social-media livestream — present-day evidence that Driver 1's print-and-itinerancy mechanism persists in networked form.
s: Asbury University, 'The Outpouring Story of Revival'; Religion News Service, 28 Feb 2023. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: The communications family (theology of the New Birth + print/itinerancy + the descendant of transatlantic networks) and democratization are the leading, durable, portable drivers likely to dominate the next phase of American revivalist religion; disestablishment, the market revolution, and the frontier are lagging — time-bound or empirically contested conditions that have largely lapsed.
s: Document synthesis grounded in sources [1]-[26] above. Accessed 2026-06-19.

claims.t: Edwards's A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God (1737) is a restrained, observational anatomy of staged conversion (with the Hutchinson and Bartlet case studies) that, circulating transatlantically before the 1740s revivals, became the template for the revival-narrative genre.
s: Edwards, A Faithful Narrative (1737), in Works vol. 4, ed. Goen (Yale UP, 1972); Jonathan Edwards Center, edwards.yale.edu (accessed 2026-06-19, site cert expired). Britannica entry corroborates the p

claims.t: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741, text Deut. 32:35) does not end in unbroken terror: its Application turns to an open offer of mercy — "Christ has thrown the door of mercy wide open" — making the terror instrumental, and its reputation as Edwards's and the revival's representative text is a later anthology-driven caricature.
s: Edwards, 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741), Blue Letter Bible transcription (accessed 2026-06-19); Works vol. 22 (Yale 2003); Ahlstrom, A Religious History of the American People (1972), a

claims.t: The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God (1741) takes as its text 1 John 4:1 (not 1 Corinthians), and argues that bodily effects, outcries, faintings, errors, and irregularities are NO evidence either way, while the genuine marks are esteem of Christ, opposition to Satan's kingdom, regard for Scripture, leading to truth, and love.
s: Edwards, The Distinguishing Marks (1741), in Works vol. 4 ed. Goen; transcription at biblebb.com/files/edwards/je-marksofhs.htm (accessed 2026-06-19).

claims.t: A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections (1746) argues 'True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections,' lists twelve signs that are 'no certain' marks either way (including bodily effects, intensity, fluent talk, scripture texts coming to mind, assurance), and gives twelve positive signs, the weightiest being Christian practice ('the chief of all the signs of grace').
s: Edwards, Religious Affections (1746), Works vol. 2, ed. John E. Smith (Yale, 1959); summaries via The Gospel Coalition and edwards.yale.edu (accessed 2026-06-19).

claims.t: Edwards's discernment works position him between the radical enthusiasts and the rationalist critics by the symmetric claim that bodily effects prove a work neither false (against Chauncy) nor true (against the enthusiasts) — relocating the test from the phenomena to the object, humility, and practice of the affected soul.
s: Edwards, Distinguishing Marks (1741) and Religious Affections (1746), Works vols. 4 and 2 (Yale); reading consistent with Smith and Goen editorial introductions.

claims.t: Whitefield's Journals and 'The Marks of the New Birth' present a religion of real inward regeneration by the Holy Spirit over against nominal Christianity (baptism, churchgoing, mere morality), with the famous Kingswood image of 'white gutters made by their tears' on the colliers' black cheeks.
s: Whitefield, 'The Marks of the New Birth' (CBN transcription, accessed 2026-06-19); George Whitefield's Journals (Banner of Truth, 1960, after Wale 1905), Quinta Press digital edition.

claims.t: The epigram 'the world is my parish' belongs to John Wesley (who wrote 'I look upon all the world as my parish' in June 1739), not George Whitefield, to whom it is routinely misattributed; and the line 'field-preaching is my plan ... carried as on eagles' wings' attributed to Whitefield cannot be pinned to a specific dated source and should be cited as characteristic rather than verified.
s: John Wesley, Journal, 11 June 1739; discussion of attribution in The Gospel Coalition Australia and Acton Institute pieces; Crossway '10 Things About Whitefield' (the unsourced 'eagles' wings' quote).

claims.t: Chauncy's Seasonable Thoughts (1743) — written as the reply to Edwards's Some Thoughts (1742) — mounts the strongest contemporary case against the revival on a division between the unreliable 'passions' and the authoritative 'understanding/reason,' attacking itinerancy, lay/female exhorters, judging others' souls, and terror preaching, and denying that good effects prove a good cause.
s: Chauncy, Seasonable Thoughts (Boston, 1743), Internet Archive; Chauncy, Enthusiasm Described and Caution'd Against (1742), Evans/Univ. of Michigan quod.lib.umich.edu (accessed 2026-06-19).

claims.t: Barton Stone's memoir gives a firsthand classification of the Cane Ridge (Aug. 1801) bodily exercises — falling, jerks, dancing, barking, laughing/singing, running — describing the jerks in detail and rendering a cautious affirmative verdict that genuine spiritual fruit followed despite 'eccentricities and much fanaticism.
s: Barton W. Stone, The Biography of Eld. Barton Warren Stone, Written by Himself (Cincinnati, 1847); excerpts at blog.richmond.edu/jerkshistory (accessed 2026-06-19).

claims.t: Taylor's Concio ad Clerum (1828, text Eph. 2:3) defines depravity not as an inherited sinful nature or substance but as 'man's own act,' with 'by nature' meaning humans will certainly-but-freely sin, preserving a 'power to the contrary' — a New Haven theology move that both claims Edwardsean descent and reaches an un-Edwardsean conclusion on inability.
s: Nathaniel W. Taylor, Concio ad Clerum (New Haven, 1828), text at gospeltruth.net/concio.htm (accessed 2026-06-19); Encyclopedia.com biography corroborates the doctrine.

claims.t: Finney's Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835, opening text Hab. 3:2) declares that a revival 'is not a miracle, or dependent on a miracle, in any sense' but 'a purely philosophical result of the right use of the constituted means,' compares it to a crop produced by agricultural means (even more reliably), and prescribes the 'new measures' (anxious seat, protracted meetings, women praying in mixed assemblies).
s: Charles G. Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835), CCEL transcription ccel.org/ccel/finney/revivals (accessed 2026-06-19); critical ed. W. G. McLoughlin (Harvard/Belknap, 1960).

claims.t: The 1784 Christmas Conference Doctrines and Discipline adopted a rule barring Methodists from buying, selling, or holding slaves (framing slavery as an 'abomination'), but that rule was suspended within roughly six months at the 1785 Baltimore Conference under southern pressure — so the Discipline read in isolation overstates early Methodism's antislavery resolve.
s: Doctrines and Discipline of the Methodist Episcopal Church (1784/85); UMC.org 'Doctrinal Standards in American Methodism' and UMNews historical accounts (accessed 2026-06-19).

claims.t: Peter Cartwright's Autobiography (1856) gives a vivid firsthand account of the 'jerks' — involuntary convulsions worsened by resistance, fashionable women's loose hair cracking 'almost as loud as a wagoner's whip,' and a cursing drunkard who took the jerks, could not drink, and 'snapped his neck' — rendered as moral tales vindicating the revival against scoffers.
s: Peter Cartwright, Autobiography of Peter Cartwright (1856), ed. Strickland; excerpt at blog.richmond.edu/jerkshistory (accessed 2026-06-19); National Humanities Center PDF.

claims.t: Richard Allen's Life, Experience, and Gospel Labours (1833) narrates his conversion in Exodus/Acts liberation idiom ('my dungeon shook, my chains flew off') and the walkout from St. George's Methodist Church after Black worshippers were pulled up off their knees in the segregated gallery — grounding both the revival's appeal to Black converts and white revivalism's enforced racial subordination.
s: Richard Allen, The Life, Experience, and Gospel Labours (Philadelphia, 1833), Documenting the American South, docsouth.unc.edu/neh/allen/allen.html (accessed 2026-06-19); Albert J. Raboteau, Slave Rel

claims.t: The date of the St. George's walkout is contested: traditionally 1787, but argued by some historians for 1792-93 near the new church's groundbreaking, and Allen's memoir (written decades later) is imprecise on the year.
s: Discussion in scholarship on Allen (Project MUSE review; docsouth.unc.edu summary; EBSCO Research Starter), accessed 2026-06-19. The revisionist dating is single-sourced here pending the specific mono

claims.t: Read in sequence, the texts trace a theological arc from Edwards's sovereign God who 'surprises' Northampton (1737), to Taylor's free agent with 'power to the contrary' (1828), to Finney's revival that is 'not a miracle' but the producible result of means (1835) — the continuity-language/rupture-theology tension underlying the two Awakenings' relation.
s: Synthesis of Edwards, Faithful Narrative (1737); Taylor, Concio ad Clerum (1828); Finney, Lectures (1835) — all cited above.

claims.t: None of the primary texts describes a unified, self-aware national 'Great Awakening': participants wrote of 'the late surprising work,' 'the present state of religion,' or 'the great revival' in particular places; the capitalized unified event is a later historians' construction.
s: Edwards, Faithful Narrative / Some Thoughts; Chauncy, Seasonable Thoughts (title); Stone, Biography — all cited above; framing consistent with Jon Butler's historiographical critique.

claims.t: OpenRTB, the open protocol standardizing programmatic bid requests/responses, was assembled by the OpenRTB Consortium in November 2010 (DSPs DataXu, MediaMath, Turn; SSPs AdMeld, PubMatic, Rubicon, ContextWeb), with a unified OpenRTB 2.0 in June 2011 and IAB adoption as a standard (v2.1) in January 2012; it remains the live lingua franca of open-market programmatic in 2026.
s: IAB Tech Lab, 'OpenRTB (Real-Time Bidding),' iabtechlab.com/standards/openrtb/, accessed 2026-06-20; cross-checked vs. pubscale.com OpenRTB guide.

claims.t: OpenRTB's tmax field caps how long an exchange waits for a bid including internet latency; SSPs typically set 80–120ms (Google historically ~100ms), a buyer responding late is dropped, and with 25–30 DSPs per auction engineers target ~70ms to protect tail latency — making cross-internet round-trip a structural 'latency tax.
s: OpenRTB v3.0 spec + docs.prebid.org/features/timeouts.html + adtechexplained.com 'Programmatic Timeouts Explained,' accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Header bidding — placing JavaScript in the page header so a publisher solicits simultaneous bids from multiple SSPs before calling the ad server — emerged in 2014 and was named/popularized by a 2015 AdExchanger article, replacing the sequential 'waterfall' and breaking Google's 'last look' advantage.
s: setupad.com 'What is Header Bidding'; AdExchanger (2015) 'The Rise of Header Bidding…' as recounted; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The header-bidding 'wrapper' — the software orchestrating simultaneous bidder calls in the browser — is also called a 'container,' marking the first use of 'container' in programmatic vocabulary; the dominant wrapper Prebid.js launched in 2015 as an open-source collaboration originated by AppNexus, governed today by the independent Prebid.org.
s: Prebid.org, 'Introduction to Prebid for Header Bidding,' docs.prebid.org/overview/intro.html, accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Google's DoubleClick exchange held a 'last look' advantage (it could see and beat the top competing bid), a key grievance driving header bidding; a leaked April-2015 Google deck 'Why first look is crucial' stated first look gives 'access to the most valuable cookies'; Google discontinued Last Look in 2018.
s: MarTech 'Countering header bidding, Google drops its last look advantage'; AdMonsters 'Last Stand for Google's Last Look'; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: AppNexus launched Prebid Server, a free open-source server-side header-bidding solution, on May 3, 2017, moving the multi-bidder auction out of the browser into a data center to cut browser calls and manage latency; Facebook joined the server-to-server drive framed against Google's dominance.
s: PRNewswire/AppNexus, 'AppNexus Launches Prebid Server' (2017-05); The Drum (2017-05-03); accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Supply-path optimization (SPO) — buyers deliberately pruning which SSPs/exchanges/resellers they transact through — had its 'first inning' around 2017 in response to header bidding's path explosion; examples include Goodway Group cutting SSPs from ~20 to single digits, GroupM's Premium Marketplace, and The Trade Desk's OpenPath, concentrating supply into a few large SSP fabrics.
s: AdExchanger, 'AdExplainer: What Is Supply-Path Optimization (SPO)?', accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Public-cloud egress fees (≈$0.09/GB AWS internet egress, ≈$0.12/GB GCP premium, $0.01/GB cross-AZ; ~6–12% of cloud bills) make high-volume remote bidding costly; because each bid request evaluated carries a real per-request cost, DSPs impose a queries-per-second (QPS) ceiling and historically processed only ~20–30% of the available bidstream.
s: spendark.com / egresscost.com 2026 egress guides; PPC Land 'Bedrock becomes first DSP…' (Naglak quote) and Index Cloud coverage; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Index Exchange CEO Andrew Casale characterized the per-request infrastructure cost of remote bidding as a 'cloud tax,' the elimination of which is containerized bidding's core economic pitch.
s: PPC Land, 'Index Cloud, Meta CTV, and synthetic audiences,' accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The modern DSP bidder is an ML model ingesting 200+ features per auction that must complete inference in roughly under 5ms within the sub-100ms window, and whose accuracy improves with proximity to fresh SSP-held signal — creating a structural pull to run inside the exchange.
s: madgicx.com 'Deploy ML Models for RTB'; Geomotiv agentic-bidding piece; AdExchanger/PPC Land Zillow coverage; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Containerized bidding packages a buyer's bidding logic as an OCI/Docker container and deploys it inside the SSP/exchange's own compute fabric co-located with the auction — inverting OpenRTB by moving the buyer to the request rather than the request to the buyer; IAB CEO Tony Katsur framed the need as 'containerize the architecture' so demand and supply no longer ping across separate data centers.
s: AdExchanger 'IAB Tech Lab Releases First Framework…' (Katsur); PPC Land Bedrock & Decision Fabric pieces; Index Exchange 'Introducing Index Cloud'; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Index Exchange's Index Cloud — a proprietary compute environment explicitly 'not built on GCP, AWS, or Azure' — entered beta on April 21, 2026 with Bedrock Platform as the first containerized DSP (sub-5ms execution window, cryptographically signed containers); partners include Chalice AI, inPowered AI, and Nano Interactive, and Index describes it as 'live today' as of its April–May 2026 announcements.
s: Index Exchange, 'Introducing Index Cloud' (2026-04-21) and Bedrock press release; ExchangeWire (2026-04-24); PPC Land; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: PubMatic launched Decision Fabric on June 1, 2026 — a layer letting DSPs, curators, and algorithm firms deploy proprietary AI models as OCI/Docker containers inside PubMatic's auction, returning segment IDs in under 10ms; inPowered is live and Chalice AI is onboarding, against PubMatic's stated 2.7 trillion daily advertiser bid requests.
s: PPC Land, 'PubMatic puts partner AI models inside the auction with Decision Fabric' (author Punit Shah, PubMatic), accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: IAB Tech Lab's Agentic RTB Framework (ARTF) v1.0, which standardizes containerized agent services running inside host infrastructure and targets up to 80% reduction in bid request/response time, opened for public comment Nov 13 2025–Jan 15 2026; the umbrella AAMP was named Feb 26 2026; and Amazon Ads donated its Dynamic Traffic Engine to the IAB open-source project on April 15 2026.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF press release; AdExchanger; PPC Land 'IAB names AAMP'; IAB/AdExchanger DTE donation coverage; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The first brand-advertiser test of containerized RTB — Zillow hosting Chalice AI's buying model inside Index Exchange to access granular site-quality signals (ad-to-content ratio, default video sound, refresh rates, data-broker calls) not present in standard bid requests — was reported August 6, 2025.
s: AdExchanger 'Zillow Pilots Containerized RTB'; PPC Land; Canvas Worldwide; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The IAB Tech Lab's ARTF treats containerized/agentic bidding as an evolution layered on OpenRTB, while the rival Ad Context Protocol (AdCP), launched October 2025 by Scope3, Yahoo, PubMatic, Swivel, Triton, and Optable, treats agentic trading as a clean-slate paradigm; as of the IAB's Feb 2026 leadership meeting it was 'unclear to what extent the two frameworks are compatible or competitive,' and the camps overlap (PubMatic, Optable appear on both sides).
s: PPC Land 'IAB names AAMP'; The Current 'IAB Tech Lab, not a fan of AdCP'; Digiday 'AdCP vs. IAB Tech Lab' (2026-02-17, Tim Peterson); accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Whoever defines the container interface, host/agent security boundary, and signaling layer (e.g., where Amazon's DTE fits) shapes which party owns the compute fabric and therefore captures margin once buyer logic moves in-exchange — making the protocol contest a proxy for the commercial take-rate question.
s: Synthesis over IAB ARTF/DTE coverage and Optable/First Party Capital margin framing; accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: In containerized bidding the OCI/Docker image carries the buyer's bidding logic — increasingly a trained ML model plus inference code, feature engineering, and bid-shaping rules — deployed as the buyer's own 'models, data, and logic in isolated infrastructure adjacent to the transaction.
s: Index Exchange, 'Index Cloud — Purpose-built for Programmatic' product page (accessed 20 Jun 2026); ExchangeWire, 24 Apr 2026; PPC Land (Apr 2026).

claims.t: ARTF defines a host platform (SSP/exchange/DSP/ad server running the auction) that runs first/third-party 'agent services' packaged as standardized lightweight containers co-located in its own infrastructure for low-latency execution.
s: ARTF Specs, 'Technical Specs,' artf.ai (accessed 20 Jun 2026); IAB Tech Lab ARTF standards page; AdExchanger 13 Nov 2025; Digiday 13 Nov 2025.

claims.t: The lifecycle is deploy-once (sign image, host verifies, container provisioned warm on Kubernetes) then invoke-per-impression via a gRPC method (GetMutations(RTBRequest) returns RTBResponse, port 50051) using Protocol Buffers; the agent returns an OpenRTB Patch of atomic 'mutations' tagged with intents that the host can accept or reject individually.
s: IABTechLab/agentic-realtime-framework, GitHub (accessed 20 Jun 2026); ARTF Specs technical material, artf.ai.

claims.t: Index Exchange's Index Cloud, launched 21 April 2026, is an in-exchange container runtime that Index states runs in its own global data centers with no GCP/AWS/Azure dependency, executing a partner container's impression-level decision in under five milliseconds before the bid request is sent to DSPs.
s: Index Exchange, 'Introducing Index Cloud,' 21 Apr 2026 and Index Cloud product page; PPC Land Apr 2026; ExchangeWire 24 Apr 2026; Mi3 28 Apr 2026.

claims.t: Most live containerized-bidding pilots are sandboxed execution environments (bring your model as an executable; the container sees only the host's rationed bidstream signals, not freely ingested buy-side first-party data) rather than true open compute fabrics — 'Snowpark, not Docker' — and 'you can't yet bring in buy-side data freely,' which constrains the architecture's larger promises.
s: Dan Jaye (CTO, Aqfer), 'Containerized RTB and How It Shifts the Programmatic Space,' aqfer.com (accessed 20 Jun 2026); cf. AdExchanger 16 Jun 2026 (Hyundai/OpenX).

claims.t: ARTF's isolation rests on agents running with 'no external network access — all network ingress and egress prohibited except for service communications with the orchestrating entity,' plus cryptographic image signing and non-root/read-only-filesystem container hardening; ARTF v1.0 does NOT require a hardware Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), unlike adjacent privacy architectures (Google confidential matching, Privacy Sandbox Bidding & Auction) that do.
s: Miguel Morales, IAB Tech Lab 'Breaking Down the Walls' blueprint (accessed 20 Jun 2026); IABTechLab/agentic-realtime-framework GitHub; AdExchanger 'Google Ads Will Now Use A TEE By Default'…

claims.t: The architecture protects the buyer's model IP (the host receives outputs/decisions, not the model source; the image is signed; the buyer retains full control of its decisioning) and the host's data (egress lockdown prevents the container exfiltrating bidstream data), with all agent inputs and outputs mediated and audited by the host under a 'least data' principle.
s: Index Exchange press release 21 Apr 2026; PPC Land Apr 2026; ExchangeWire 24 Apr 2026; ARTF Specs technical material; AdExchanger 13 Nov 2025 (Katsur).

claims.t: QPS (queries-per-second) throttling exists because each bid request carries a real per-request egress/processing cost; co-locating the bidder inside the cluster drops that cost to near zero, letting the bidder evaluate every impression on a deal rather than a throttled sampled slice.
s: Damian Naglak (Bedrock), in PPC Land, Apr 2026; corroborating egress economics: AWS RTB Fabric blog 16 Jun 2026; egresscost.com / PPC Land.

claims.t: By eliminating the bid-request round-trip and its egress cost, containerized bidding produces 'a shift in the cost curve of programmatic buying, reducing the dependency between infrastructure spend and market access' — a small buyer's container can see every impression on a deal without paying internet-scale ingest costs, so scale is no longer limited to the largest DSPs.
s: Index Exchange press release 21 Apr 2026; ExchangeWire 24 Apr 2026 (Casale, Shevlin).

claims.t: A mid-size exchange generates on the order of 8.64 billion bid requests/day at ~3KB each (~725 TB monthly egress) with roughly 90% resulting in no-bids; public-cloud egress runs ~$0.09–$0.12/GB, and attacking this round-trip yields documented 80%+ networking cost savings (AWS RTB Fabric reports 84% DSP / 65% SSP reductions, shifting pricing from per-byte to per-transaction).
s: AWS, 'Next-generation programmatic advertising: How AWS RTB Fabric redefines the game,' industries blog, 16 Jun 2026; cloud egress pricing data via egresscost.com / PPC Land (accessed 20 Jun 2026).

claims.t: OpenX's OpenXBuild ('Custom Decisioning') runs buy-side models as always-on bidding agents within OpenX's infrastructure, but OpenX is built entirely on Google Cloud Platform, so OpenX (the host) pays for the greater cloud bandwidth the containers consume — a different cost structure from Index, which owns its data centers; OpenX CTO Joel Meyer argues that hosting cost is still smaller than the egress cost of sending the bid request out to DSPs.
s: James Hercher, 'Hyundai Tests Containerized Ad Tech To Drive New Efficiency,' AdExchanger, 16 Jun 2026.

claims.t: In the OpenX/Chalice AI/Hyundai pilot, the container lets the buyer bid on 'data signals and other factors that aren't in the bidstream' — Hyundai feeding proprietary 'high-value actions' (e.g., dealership test-drives) as conversion signals and wanting to own its targeting model — representing the sandbox cracking open toward buyer first-party data; the campaign reportedly delivered a 20% reduction in cost per high-value action and a 67% CPM decrease vs the next-best alternative (figures claimed in a Business Wire press release, not independently verified).
s: AdExchanger, 16 Jun 2026 (Gilpin/Meyer); Business Wire 'Chalice AI and OpenX Bring AI-Powered Curation to High-Quality Video,' 16 Jun 2026 (via Yahoo Finance / MarTech Series).

claims.t: ARTF targets reducing bid request/response times by up to ~80% — from typical 400–800ms (Katsur cites 400–600ms) down to roughly 100ms — with the in-fabric agent call itself targeting sub-millisecond response, because data and compute are in the same data center/server/VM and there is no internet round-trip.
s: ARTF Specs technical material, artf.ai; IAB Tech Lab blueprint; AdExchanger 13 Nov 2025; PR Newswire 13 Nov 2025.

claims.t: ARTF v1.0 was released for public comment 13 Nov 2025; the window closed 15 Jan 2026; as of June 2026 it is described as soon-to-be-finalized with v2.0 already underway, and it sits under the AAMP umbrella (since ~Mar 2026) extending rather than replacing OpenRTB/AdCOM/VAST/GPP/TCF — so present-tense claims that ARTF 'is the standard' are premature.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF standards page (accessed 20 Jun 2026); PR Newswire 13 Nov 2025; IAB UK agentic-standards explainer; IAB Tech Lab 2026 roadmap.

claims.t: Because each SSP can stand up its own container fabric, a buyer may have to deploy separate containers into Index Cloud, OpenXBuild, and every other exchange, and 'once every SSP spins up its own container, frequency management and deduplication get messy' — a structural friction that could erode the efficiency gains and create a bidding-against-yourself risk.
s: Dan Jaye (CTO, Aqfer), 'Containerized RTB and How It Shifts the Programmatic Space,' aqfer.com (accessed 20 Jun 2026).

claims.t: The IAB Tech Lab Agentic Real-Time Framework (ARTF) is the spec that standardizes the container/host-platform pattern for containerized bidding — packaging a participant's logic as a container and running it inside the auction host's own data center.
s: IAB Tech Lab, 'IAB Tech Lab Announces Agentic RTB Framework (ARTF) v1.0 for Public Comment,' PRNewswire/iabtechlab.com, Nov 13, 2025, accessed 2026-06-20; artf.ai; iabtechlab.com 'Breaking Down the Walls.

claims.t: ARTF v1.0 was released for public comment on November 13, 2025, with an extended comment period that closed January 15, 2026; as of April 2026 the IAB page shows v1.0 finalized/finalizing and v2.0 'underway,' with no confirmed published v2.0 found through June 2026.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF press release Nov 13 2025 and ARTF standards page (iabtechlab.com/standards/artf/, last updated Feb 18 2026), accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: ARTF's stated 'up to 80% / ~600-800ms to ~100ms' latency reduction is an IAB Tech Lab design target attributed to the Tech Lab, with no published independent benchmark; the Lab's own materials cite mutually inconsistent figures (~100ms end-to-end vs Index Exchange's '<10ms' vs blueprint's 'sub-millisecond') and an inconsistent baseline (400-600 / 400-800 / 600-800ms).
s: IAB Tech Lab press release Nov 13 2025; MarTech Nov 13 2025; AdExchanger Nov 2025; artf.ai/technical-specs; Index Exchange Index Explains; iabtechlab.com 'Breaking Down the Walls' — all accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: ARTF extends rather than replaces OpenRTB, AdCOM, and VAST: agentic action is expressed as 'OpenRTB Patch' deltas against the existing bid object, keeping the bidstream and existing IAB taxonomies central — characterized by the IAB as 'evolution, not revolution' and enabling agentic execution 'without rebuilding the market's foundational languages.
s: artf.ai/technical-specs; IAB Tech Lab Agentic Roadmap (iabtechlab.com, Jan 6 2026); IAB UK roadmap explainer — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: On February 26, 2026, IAB Tech Lab formally named its umbrella agentic initiative AAMP (Agentic Advertising Management Protocols), authored by CEO Anthony Katsur, explicitly to end 'confusion in the market' caused by observers treating ARTF and Agentic Audiences as the sum total of its agentic work; AAMP has three pillars (Agentic Foundations/execution, Agentic Protocols/management, Trust & Transparency) and positions ARTF as its execution pillar.
s: IAB Tech Lab, 'Framing the Agentic Advertising Management Protocols (AAMP) Initiative,' Feb 26 2026; AAMP standards page (iabtechlab.com)…

claims.t: AAMP reached version 2.0 on April 29, 2026 with transaction-ready Buyer and Seller Agent SDKs; the most recent IAB page reviewed (Apr 23 2026) shows AAMP 2.0 as current, and no published AAMP 3.0 was confirmed through June 2026 (it is referenced only as 'underway').
s: IAB Tech Lab, 'AAMP 2.0 Release Brings Transaction-ready Buyer and Seller Agent SDKs,' Apr 29 2026; AAMP standards page (iabtechlab.com, updated Apr 23 2026) — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The ARTF-vs-AdCP split is fundamentally about market topology and margin, not engineering: ARTF 'accelerates the existing pipes, keeps DSPs central' and preserves the supply chain, while AdCP has 'seller agents negotiate directly with buyer agents, compressing the supply chain and shifting margin toward publishers and the SSPs that orchestrate them' — 'not a technical disagreement... a fight over who sits in the middle of the next decade of advertising.
s: Broadbrand, 'The Protocol War Between ARTF and AdCP Splits Agentic Adtech,' accessed 2026-06-20; corroborated by Digiday 'WTF is Ad Context Protocol (AdCP)?' Oct 15 2025; PubMatic 'Moving Beyond AdCP vs ARTF.

claims.t: Containerized bidding is definitionally the ARTF answer to agentic media buying — it presupposes the auction remains central and gains efficiency by co-locating compute with it — whereas AdCP's topology routes around the impression-level auction, making the two architectures pull in opposite long-run directions even if they compose at different layers short-run.
s: Author's synthesis of artf.ai spec, Digiday AdCP explainer (Oct 15 2025), Broadbrand 'Protocol War,' and PubMatic 'Moving Beyond AdCP vs ARTF' — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: AdCP (Ad Context Protocol) is an open standard launched October 2025 by a Scope3-led coalition of 20+ ad-tech firms (founding members Optable, PubMatic, Scope3, Swivel, Triton Digital, Yahoo; notably excluding The Trade Desk, DV360, and Amazon DSP), built on Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) and A2A frameworks, standardizing how buyer and seller agents negotiate media deals directly.
s: Digiday, 'WTF is Ad Context Protocol (AdCP)?' Oct 15 2025; Samba TV 'Industry Coalition Launches Ad Context Protocol (AdCP)'; MobileMarketingReads AdCP launch coverage — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: IAB Tech Lab CEO Anthony Katsur, in the January 6, 2026 agentic roadmap, said 'the industry should expect several false starts in deploying agentic solutions' and argued 'the fastest and smartest way forward is to build on an existing shared foundation, not introduce multiple new standards that create fragmentation'; he is cold on AdCP, having said the industry did not need 'another trade group' and that the Tech Lab already addresses what AdCP claims to solve.
s: IAB Tech Lab, 'IAB Tech Lab Unveils Agentic Roadmap,' Jan 6 2026; The Current, 'IAB Tech Lab announces an agentic roadmap, but don't expect any love for AdCP' — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: PubMatic — an SSP whose leaders sit on the boards of IAB, IAB Tech Lab, and Prebid.org and which was a founding AdCP member — argues ARTF and AdCP are complementary layers, not rivals ('the real question is not whether one approach replaces the other, but how platforms... navigate coexistence without fragmenting the market'), with AdCP at the application/negotiation layer and ARTF at the transaction/execution layer.
s: PubMatic, 'Moving Beyond AdCP vs ARTF: How Both Power Agentic Advertising,' accessed 2026-06-20; Spyrosoft AdTech explainer.

claims.t: ARTF's protocol is asymmetric by design — containers return proposed OpenRTB Patch mutations tagged with declared intents, but the host platform decides which to apply and the container cannot unilaterally change the auction ('propose, don't decide') — which critics argue means 'agentic' is overstated and the design entrenches incumbent host control.
s: artf.ai/technical-specs and ARTF spec PDF; Index Exchange 'Index Explains'; Amit Goel, bidstream.amitgoel.me, Jun 3 2026 — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: ARTF is governed by IAB Tech Lab via open public comment and public GitHub repositories, but its working group is populated by the platforms that benefit as container hosts (Index Exchange, Chalice, The Trade Desk, CTV-heavy sellers); the headline interoperability risk is fragmentation, since two competing specs (ARTF and AdCP) advance under separate stewards with no guaranteed interoperability.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF press release Nov 13 2025; ARTF standards page; Samba TV AdCP release; IAB roadmap Jan 6 2026 — accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Index Exchange announced Index Cloud, a proprietary in-exchange compute environment hosting buyer containers, on April 21, 2026, and as of that announcement it is in closed beta with select partners.
s: Index Exchange, 'Introducing Index Cloud,' indexexchange.com, Apr 21 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Index Cloud runs on infrastructure Index Exchange owns and operates itself rather than on a public cloud (GCP, AWS, or Azure).
s: Index Exchange, 'Introducing Index Cloud,' Apr 21 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Bedrock Platform became the first DSP to run its complete bidder as a container inside an exchange (Index Cloud), debuting April 21-24, 2026.
s: PPC Land, 'Bedrock becomes first DSP to run its bidder inside an exchange,' Apr 2026; Index/Bedrock releases (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Bedrock Platform is a London-headquartered, model-driven DSP (CEO Shane Shevlin, eng. head Damian Naglak) whose pitch is that the architecture lets a non-giant compete without infrastructure scale.
s: PPC Land, Apr 2026; Bedrock Platform release (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: First containerized DSP' means Bedrock deployed its complete decisioning and bidding logic, a full bidder, not merely an audience or optimization model, inside the SSP, distinguishing it from segment-ID models like PubMatic's Decision Fabric.
s: PPC Land, 'Bedrock becomes first DSP...,' Apr 2026; PPC Land, 'PubMatic puts partner AI models inside the auction,' Jun 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Index named Chalice AI, inPowered AI, and Nano Interactive as Index Cloud partners and InterMedia Group, Bay Street Media, and Navigator as among the first to test the Bedrock integration.
s: Index Exchange, 'Introducing Index Cloud,' Apr 21 2026; Bedrock Platform release (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: PubMatic launched Decision Fabric, a containerization layer on its AgenticOS, on June 1, 2026, running partner decisioning models inside its supply path and returning segment IDs into curated deals.
s: PubMatic Inc., 'PubMatic Launches Decision Fabric on AgenticOS,' BusinessWire, Jun 1 2026; PPC Land, Jun 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: PubMatic's release names four Decision Fabric pilot partners (inPowered AI, MiQ, Chalice AI, SWYM.AI), but independent PPC Land reporting describes only inPowered as 'live' and Chalice as 'onboarding,' with no mention of MiQ or SWYM.AI.
s: PubMatic Inc. release, Jun 1 2026; PPC Land, 'PubMatic puts partner AI models inside the auction,' Jun 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: PubMatic named MiQ, a large independent cross-DSP trading desk, as a Decision Fabric pilot partner bringing buyer-side trading intelligence inside the supply path, signaling cross-DSP intelligence can relocate into the SSP fabric.
s: PubMatic Inc., 'PubMatic Launches Decision Fabric on AgenticOS,' BusinessWire, Jun 1 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: OpenX, which repositioned as 'The Intelligent SSP' on April 14, 2026, runs a containerized-bidding product called OpenXBuild, with Hyundai testing Chalice AI's model through it across three vehicles; OpenX (on Google Cloud Platform) bears the bandwidth cost.
s: AdExchanger, 'Hyundai Tests Containerized Ad Tech To Drive New Efficiency,' 2026; OpenX/ExchangeWire rebrand release, Apr 14 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: In August 2025, Zillow (via agency Canvas Worldwide) ran Chalice Custom Algorithms' buying model inside Index Exchange's servers, the first independently reported live containerized-RTB deployment, predating the 'Index Cloud' brand, to access site-level quality signals.
s: AdExchanger, 'Zillow Pilots Containerized RTB...,' Aug 6 2025; Canvas Worldwide release (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: On April 15, 2026, Amazon Ads donated its Dynamic Traffic Engine, a file-based system letting DSPs signal bidding priorities to SSPs to cut QPS waste, to IAB Tech Lab as open source, a protocol-layer alternative to co-locating a bidder.
s: IAB Tech Lab/PRNewswire, Apr 15 2026; AdExchanger, 'Amazon Ads Hands The IAB Tech Lab A Tool...,' Apr 15 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: As of mid-2026 none of the major independent or walled-garden DSPs (The Trade Desk, Yahoo, Google DV360, Amazon) runs its core bidder inside a rival open-web SSP's compute fabric; they build agentic capability on their own stacks instead.
s: Digiday, May 5 2026; AdTechRadar/MediaPost Yahoo CES Jan 2026; Google DV360 OpenRTB spec (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Yahoo DSP, the most forward-leaning incumbent on agentic buying, embraces external orchestration layers while keeping data, decisioning, optimization, and measurement proprietary, positioning as the 'system of record'; it is also an AdCP founding member.
s: Digiday, 'Yahoo pairs with Kochava to pitch agentic DSP workflows,' May 5 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Chalice AI runs inside Index Cloud, OpenXBuild, and PubMatic Decision Fabric (and ran the Zillow pilot inside Index), and inPowered AI runs inside Index Marketplaces and Decision Fabric, making them platform-independent vendors across competing fabrics.
s: Index release Apr 21 2026; AdExchanger Hyundai 2026; PPC Land Jun 2026; Index 'inPowered fastest-growing' Oct 22 2025 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Magnite, a large independent SSP and ARTF Container Project member, has signaled hybrid-infrastructure readiness and offers the ClearLine direct-booking product but has not shipped an Index-Cloud-equivalent containerized-bidding product of its own as of mid-2026.
s: Magnite, 'The Elastic Edge...' blog 2026 (fetch blocked, via search); ExchangeWire 'A New Type of DSP Is Emerging,' Jun 17 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: A new 'direct DSP'/'Direct Booking Engine' category, of which Index Cloud, PubMatic Activate, and Magnite ClearLine are named variants, competes on dramatically lower take rates than established DSPs, pushing margin toward publishers and agencies.
s: ExchangeWire, 'A New Type of DSP Is Emerging,' Jun 17 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: By hosting buyer logic, the SSP becomes not just an exchange but the compute-and-data environment in which AI-driven decisioning happens, a new value-chain seat and potential lock-in point.
s: PPC Land, 'PubMatic puts partner AI models inside the auction with Decision Fabric,' Jun 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: The IAB Tech Lab ARTF Container Project working group includes Index Exchange, OpenX, The Trade Desk, and Chalice as core contributors plus Amazon Ads, Netflix, Yahoo, Paramount, Optable, HUMAN Security, Magnite, PubMatic, WPP Media, and Basis Technologies.
s: Adweek, 'IAB Launches Technical Standard...,' 2025; PPC Land ARTF coverage (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Containerized bidding keeps the auction, bidstream, and DSP-SSP-exchange chain central while moving compute next to the data, making it the ARTF-shaped architecture, as opposed to AdCP's direct buyer-agent/seller-agent negotiation that routes around the auction.
s: Sibling doc 03_Standards_ARTF_AAMP.md; Index and PubMatic ARTF-alignment statements 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: As of mid-2026, production containerized-bidding deployments are sandboxed execution environments in which the host controls which bid-request fields the agent sees and buyers cannot freely bring their own buy-side/first-party data in, which constrains the 'richer signal' promise.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF v1.0 Technical Specs, accessed 2026-06-20; Dan Jaye (Aqfer CTO), aqfer.com/containerized_rtb/; Zillow pilot via PPC Land/AdExchanger 2025-08-06.

claims.t: The ARTF v1.0 specification provides cryptographic image signing and host-mediated I/O but no trusted-execution-environment or confidential-compute mechanism, so the host's inability to see the agent's logic and bids is a policy promise, not a cryptographic guarantee.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF v1.0 Technical Specs (artf.ai; github.com/IABTechLab/agentic-realtime-framework), accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The ARTF v1.0 specification contains no provision for cross-host frequency capping or deduplication, and proponents concede this is unsolved: once every SSP runs its own container fabric, a multi-homing buyer makes isolated bid decisions that cannot coordinate, risking bidding against itself.
s: IAB Tech Lab ARTF v1.0 spec, accessed 2026-06-20; Dan Jaye (Aqfer CTO), aqfer.com/containerized_rtb/.

claims.t: Programmatic already suffers chronic bid duplication — the same impression offered through multiple supply paths so a buyer bids against itself — with The Trade Desk reporting SSPs 'send 30% of the publisher's traffic... and they send it three times,' and frequency caps failing to synchronize across DSPs (doubling CPMs).
s: Sarah Sluis, AdExchanger, 'Attack Of The Clones,' 2024-01-17; 'GroupM Discovers Frequency Capping Is A Data Integration Challenge,' AdExchanger.

claims.t: A November 2025 Truthset study for CIMM and Go Addressable, benchmarking ~247M IPs and 938M IP-to-postal pairs from six providers against ground truth from two ISPs and one vMVPD, found IP-to-postal linkages accurate on average 13% of the time and IP-to-email 16%.
s: Truthset for CIMM/Go Addressable, 'The Challenges of Using IP Address for Audience Identification and Measurement,' 2025-11-05 (34pp). Note: each page marked 'preliminary and subject to change.

claims.t: The Truthset/CIMM study models that, after IP error, postal error, email error, and demographic error compound, roughly $0.03 of every media dollar reaches the intended audience; providers agree with each other only 6.4% (IP-postal) and 2.8% (IP-email) of the time, with 93% of linkages unique to a single provider.
s: Truthset for CIMM/Go Addressable, 2025-11-05, pp. 21-27.

claims.t: Containerization co-locates the decisioning algorithm with the auction but is signal-agnostic — it neither improves nor worsens the underlying identity graph — so where the identity substrate is weak (probabilistic IP), a faster, closer algorithm produces faster confident error rather than better outcomes.
s: Inference from ARTF spec (architecture scope) + Truthset/CIMM 2025-11-05 (identity accuracy); proponent counter (FreeWheel 2026-02-28) concedes the IP-accuracy figure.

claims.t: The MRC's January 2026 Digital Advertising Auction Transparency Standards cover auction mechanics (auction type, floors, bid adjustments, decision variables) and explicitly not performance, incrementality, or lift; the MRC SVP confirms transparency accreditation is 'completely separate from other MRC accreditations' and incrementality standards remain under development.
s: Anthony Vargas, AdExchanger, 2026-02-03; MRC Digital Advertising Auction Transparency Standards, Jan 2026.

claims.t: Containerized-bidding performance figures (CPA/ROAS/conversion lift) are vendor-run holdout results published by firms selling the architecture, with no independent MRC or third-party accreditation available as of mid-2026, and are subject to survivorship bias in published case studies.
s: Inference from MRC standards scope (2026-01) + Adam Heimlich quote via The Current, 2025-11-13; no independent lift accreditation located as of 2026-06-20.

claims.t: As of June 2026, Index Cloud (launched 2026-04-21) is effectively the only production containerized-bidding fabric, with Bedrock the first containerized DSP (2026-04-24) deployed single-vendor on Index only, in 'closed beta with select partners' — creating present-day concentration and switching-cost risk.
s: Index Exchange, 'Introducing Index Cloud,' 2026-04-21; ExchangeWire, 2026-04-24; PPC Land, 2026-04-25; ExchangeWire, 2026-06-16.

claims.t: The ARTF Go reference implementation is copyright Index Exchange Inc. under AGPL-3.0 (the spec itself is CC-BY-3.0), giving the firm that ships the only production fabric structural influence over the standard, though formal governance sits with an IAB Tech Lab Architecture Group of multiple firms.
s: github.com/IABTechLab/agentic-realtime-framework, accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Index Exchange CEO Andrew Casale published an open letter (2023-04-19) pledging never to disintermediate DSPs or build an end-to-end platform, and reiterates a pure sell-side posture in 2026, framing containerization as a 'mini DSP renaissance' — a reassurance the neutrality critique interrogates as a voluntary, reputation-backed (not cryptographic) commitment.
s: Andrew Casale, Index Exchange open letter, 2023-04-19; ExchangeWire 2026-06-16; Beet.TV 2026-02-10.

claims.t: Containerization addresses only the open programmatic internet (~20-30% of programmatic spend); the largest walled gardens took an estimated 78% of global digital ad revenue in 2022, projected to reach 83% by 2027, capping the category's TAM and giving it a flat-to-declining market to optimize.
s: Statista, 'Walled gardens' share of digital ad revenue,' accessed 2026-06-20; corroborating eMarketer/trade analyses.

claims.t: The FTC's Mobilewalla action (Dec 2024, finalized Jan 2025) was the first time the agency alleged that collecting/retaining data from real-time bidding auctions for purposes other than participating in them is an unfair practice under Section 5, establishing a precedent that bears directly on in-stream container data access.
s: FTC, 'FTC Takes Action Against Mobilewalla...' 2024-12-03 and 'FTC Finalizes Order...' 2025-01; legal-analysis corroboration.

claims.t: The EU AI Act's GPAI obligations became applicable 2025-08-02, and AI Office enforcement powers plus Article 50 transparency obligations take effect 2026-08-02; automated ad-decisioning over personal data sits under the AI Act and GDPR concurrently, creating interpretation-dependent exposure for container-resident targeting algorithms in the EU.
s: European Commission, AI Act regulatory framework (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu), accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: In the August 2025 Zillow/Chalice/Index containerized-RTB pilot (2 clients: Zillow and one auto brand), the container analyzed supply-quality signals the SSP already held — ad ratio per page, default sound settings, refresh rates, organic video length, data-broker calls — demonstrating the sandboxed-execution limit in the field rather than first-party-data activation.
s: PPC Land, 'Zillow pilots containerized RTB...,' 2025-08-07 (on AdExchanger 2025-08-06).

claims.t: In its June 2, 2026 blog 'The Elastic Edge,' Magnite states it has 'invested significantly' in hybrid infrastructure and that 'for clients who prefer other deployment models, such as containerization, Magnite can support those needs as well.
s: Magnite, 'The Elastic Edge,' magnite.com/blog, Jun 2, 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20; 403 on fetch, recovered via search snapshot).

claims.t: The Magnite-Cognitiv integration (Jan 6, 2026) runs Cognitiv's deep-learning models inside Magnite's bidstream 'during the milliseconds…before DSPs submit bids' to 'execute closer to the impression' — functionally sell-side AI decisioning co-located with the auction, framed as curation.
s: GlobeNewswire/Magnite, Jan 6, 2026; PPC Land, Jan 8, 2026; StockTitan MGNI, Jan 6, 2026 (all accessed 2026-06-20).

claims.t: Unlike Decision Fabric or Index Cloud, ClearLine+Cognitiv is a bilateral native integration of one partner's models, not a self-serve OCI/Docker container platform with an open partner roster.
s: GlobeNewswire/Magnite Jan 6, 2026; StockTitan Jan 6, 2026; PPC Land Jan 8, 2026 (absence of container/OCI/self-deploy language across all three).

claims.t: Cognitiv is a platform-independent deep-learning ad-decisioning vendor founded in 2015 (CEO Jeremy Fain, CSO Aaron Andalman, CTO Marc Hudacsko), of the same archetype as Chalice/inPowered/SWYM, now running inside Magnite — and absent from the corpus's 04 §3.1 tenant slate.
s: BusinessWire Mar 3, 2026; cognitiv.ai/about-us; Magnite/GlobeNewswire Jan 6, 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20).

claims.t: A June 17, 2026 SWYM release states it 'is leveraging containerized deployments with top supply partners including Index Exchange, Magnite, Media.net, OpenX, and PubMatic' — these five listed as live vs. Equativ/Nexxen 'in-process' — so Magnite already hosts at least one live containerized tenant.
s: SWYM, 'SWYM Delivers AI-Powered Supply Shaping… Cross-SSP Containerization,' GlobeNewswire via Manila Times, Jun 17, 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20).

claims.t: Magnite has an 'AI buyer agent' that 'operates within Magnite's existing infrastructure,' in early tests with Kepler and MiQ on Disney inventory, plus seller-agent work with PMX (Publicis); Magnite participates in IAB Tech Lab's ARTF. Pilot stage, not GA.
s: PPC Land, 'Magnite expands AI buyer agent and SpringServe mediation with Disney and MiQ,' Apr 28, 2026 (accessed 2026-06-20).

claims.t: Magnite's Oct 1, 2025 unification of curation and activation in ClearLine put it on SpringServe's infrastructure so 'curated campaigns are executed closer to the impression' (status: 'coming soon in beta'), with AI/agentic from the Sep 9, 2025 streamr.ai acquisition.
s: GlobeNewswire/Magnite Oct 1, 2025; PPC Land Oct 2025; Magnite Sep 9, 2025 (accessed 2026-06-20).

claims.t: 04 §1.4/§3.2/§7's 'signalled readiness but not shipped a containerized-bidding product' understates Magnite's actual position; corrected status: runs third-party AI decisioning inside its auction today (Cognitiv embedded; SWYM container live; agent pilots) and supports containerized deployment, but has not productized a named open self-serve container host for a full buyer bidder.
s: Aggregates [1][2][4][7][9]; see doc body §4.

claims.t: ARTF defines an agent service as a containerized 'identity resolution, fraud detection, contextual or audience enrichment, bidding logic, or measurement' service, with native non-bidding verbs (the ADD_METRICS intent for viewability) and a sequential/parallel multi-agent orchestration model — making bidding one tenant of a building designed for an enrichment pipeline.
s: ARTF Specs technical-specs (artf.ai); IAB Tech Lab 'Breaking Down the Walls' blueprint; IABTechLab/agentic-realtime-framework GitHub — all accessed 20 Jun 2026.

claims.t: DoubleVerify is simultaneously the furthest-along containerized verification case (sell-side data in Index Exchange since Feb 27 2025; public ARTF endorsement via VP Amanda Carlton on Index's May 2026 panel) and the clearest case of category conflation — its most-publicized 'agent,' DV Neura (Jun 17 2026), is an MCP assistant on DV's own infrastructure with no mention of ARTF, containers, or in-exchange deployment.
s: DoubleVerify/Business Wire, 27 Feb 2025; Index Exchange 'Building for Programmatic's Agentic Future With ARTF,' 12 May 2026; PPC Land/MediaPost DV Neura, 17-18 Jun 2026 — all accessed 20 Jun 2026.

claims.t: As of June 2026 the fraud/verification/contextual cohort's ARTF involvement is predominantly governance and roster (HUMAN Security, Optable, Basis in the Container Project working group; GumGum and Oracle in the Architecture Group; Zefr a code contributor), not dated production container deployment with run-rate.
s: Adweek ARTF working-group roster (via search), 2025-26; IABTechLab/agentic-realtime-framework GitHub governance, accessed 20 Jun 2026.

claims.t: The two in-market proof points for fabrics beyond the celebrated Bedrock full-bidder case — the Zillow/Index supply-quality pilot (Aug 2025) and PubMatic Decision Fabric's launch tenants (Jun 1 2026) — are both non-bidding enrichment use cases (supply quality; audience qualification and inventory curation), making the full-bidder the exception rather than the modal first deployment.
s: AdExchanger/PPC Land, 6 Aug 2025; PubMatic/Business Wire/PPC Land, 1 Jun 2026; corpus 04_Market_and_Competitive_Map.md — accessed 20 Jun 2026.

claims.t: The egress-locked, host-can't-inspect container is a better fit for verification and anti-fraud IP than for bidder IP, because fraud-model secrecy is simultaneously a competitive moat and an anti-evasion security property (an exposed fraud model is an evadable one), strengthening the case that anti-fraud is a natural early tenant.
s: AdExchanger, 13 Nov 2025; Index Exchange panel recap, 12 May 2026 — accessed 20 Jun 2026; anti-evasion point is author inference.

claims.t: The 'host can't see the code' framing changes a verification vendor's deployment options and IP protection but does not resolve — and arguably sharpens — the independence/auditability problem at the core of the verification business, because measurement run inside the measured exchange, sealed from the advertiser, trades third-party transparency for privacy and collides with the vendors' own 'explainable AI / no black box' positioning.
s: IAS/PPC Land 'IAS Agent promises … without the AI black box,' 16 Dec 2025; corpus 02 OQ4 and 06 Risk 6 — accessed 20 Jun 2026; auditability synthesis is author inference.

claims.t: Available June 2026 evidence supports a reframing — the first at-scale containerized deployments are more likely non-bidding enrichment agents (fraud, contextual, supply-quality, measurement, identity) than relocated bidders — but the claim is directional, resting on use-case primacy and the non-bidders' freedom from the open-compute constraint, not on revenue data, which does not exist in the public record; the corpus's bidder-first margin story is best re-cast as Act II of a story whose Act I is trust and supply quality.
s: Synthesis of sources [1][2][3][10][12] and corpus 06 Risk 1 / 04; no public revenue figures exist — claim is explicitly directional. Accessed 20 Jun 2026.

claims.t: The largest source of programmatic advertising's carbon footprint is the real-time-bidding round-trip — the speculative, mostly-no-bid traffic that containerized bidding is designed to eliminate — corroborated by two independent measurement firms (Scope3: ~60% from 'ad selection'; Cedara: ~73% from 'auctioning calls', 87% from network utilization, ~6% from data centers).
s: Scope3 report (scope3.com) + The Drum, 19 Apr 2023; IAB Europe summarizing Cedara, May 2024 (iabeurope.eu). Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Containerized bidding adds an always-on, increasingly GPU-based compute layer inside the exchange (e.g., PubMatic's NVIDIA L40S/Triton deployment), whose net carbon impact — given embodied GPU carbon, host grid mix, and unaudited efficiency claims — has not been independently measured.
s: PubMatic/NVIDIA, 8 Oct 2025 (pubmatic.com); PubMatic 100%-renewable release; workstream 02. Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Containerized bidding's headline benefit — near-zero marginal cost to evaluate every impression, removing QPS throttling — is a direct Jevons-rebound trigger that could neutralize or invert the per-request carbon saving by incentivizing the scoring of far more impressions.
s: Luccioni, Strubell & Crawford, FAccT 2025 (arXiv:2501.16548); workstream 02 Bedrock/Naglak quote. Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: California SB 253 makes emissions disclosure mandatory for $1B+ revenue companies on a fixed schedule — Scope 1-2 by August 10, 2026, Scope 3 from 2027 (safe harbor to 2030) — converting the programmatic supply chain's carbon into a reportable, eventually-assured line item; CARB approved the regulations 26 Feb 2026 and the law is not enjoined.
s: Nixon Peabody LLP, 2 Mar 2026; CA SB-253 text (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov); CARB. Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: The ARTF-vs-AdCP topology split maps onto a carbon fault line: containerization (ARTF) reduces per-request transit while risking more requests via de-throttling, whereas AdCP compresses the supply chain and reduces the number of requests — so because programmatic carbon is dominated by request volume over the network (60-87% by independent measures), supply-chain compression may be a larger carbon lever than compute co-location.
s: Workstream 03; Greenbids via AdExchanger (Mar 2024); carbonintelligence.green (Jan 2026); Scope3/AdExchanger (Mar 2025). Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Carbon-weighted bidding formulas are claimed to achieve 22-41% emission reductions while maintaining or improving KPIs, and major DSPs now expose carbon scoring as a native bidding dimension under GMSF v1.2 factors — but the 22-41% range is attributed to unnamed 'early implementations' with no named study.
s: carbonintelligence.green, 12 Jan 2026; cross-checked vs Greenbids/AdExchanger, 4 Mar 2024. Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Optable (an AdCP founding member) frames containerized bidding as 'more sustainable economics... without needing to run global, always-on infrastructure,' but provides zero emissions data, frames sustainability purely as cost/efficiency, and does not acknowledge that resident/always-on containers relocate compute onto the host rather than eliminating it.
s: Bosko Milekic, Optable blog, 4 Aug 2025 (optable.co/blog/containerized-bidding-impact). Accessed 2026-06-20.

claims.t: Pontiac Intelligence (NY DSP, founded 2015/16, 11-50 employees, active 2026 G2/Crunchbase), Universal Ads (Comcast, launched Q1 2025, linear added Apr 27 2026), and Onetag Dynamo (launched Jun 15 2026, PE-backed parent, Aryel acquired Mar 2026) all exist and are operating as of mid-2026.
s: Crunchbase 'Pontiac Intelligence' (accessed 2026-06-20); Comcast Corporate press release 2025-01-06 + Universal Ads newsroom 2026-04-27; Onetag/ExchangeWire 2026-06-15; Tech.eu 2026-03-02

claims.t: None of Pontiac, Universal Ads, or Onetag Dynamo runs a buyer's bidder as a container co-located inside a third-party exchange's compute; each compresses fees by a non-container mechanism (own infra / publisher storefront / DSP-agnostic curation).
s: pontiac.media/media-buying (accessed 2026-06-20); Comcast press release 2025-01-06; Onetag 'Dynamo' release 2026-06-15

claims.t: The ExchangeWire source defines the Direct Booking Engine by 'transparency, supply-path integrity, and fee compression,' mentions Index Cloud only in passing and ARTF only as an 'earlier incarnation,' and never defines the DBE as a container — so the corpus's equivalence between DBE and containerized bidding over-reads the source.
s: ExchangeWire, 'A New Type of DSP Is Emerging,' 2026-06-17 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Pontiac's published self-service price is a 'fully transparent 20% Software License fee on all media purchased through the platform' — roughly The Trade Desk's ~20% platform fee — so the 'dramatically lower take rate' framing is positioning, not a verified fee delta.
s: pontiac.media/media-buying (accessed 2026-06-20); cf. TTD ~20% in corpus doc 05 §5.2 [23]

claims.t: Onetag Dynamo's '25% lower CPA with zero tech fee' is a single agency testimonial (Phil Farrington, Tomorrow: CPA down 25%, CPMs UP 12%) describing outcome optimisation / media-quality selection at the curation layer, not a take-rate reduction and not a containerization result; no methodology or holdout disclosed.
s: Onetag, 'Onetag Dynamo Delivers 25% Lower CPA...,' 2026-06-15 (accessed 2026-06-20)

claims.t: Because Universal Ads (free), Onetag Dynamo (zero buyer fee), and Pontiac (disclosed flat fee) compress the ad-tech tax without any in-exchange container, the corpus's claim that containerization is the load-bearing mechanism of fee compression is weakened — containerization (Bedrock/Index Cloud) is one route among several, distinguished by its own QPS-decoupling mechanism, not by fee compression per se.
s: Derived from claims 10.2-10.5; cross-referenced against corpus docs 04 §6.2 and 05 §5.2

claims.t: On June 17, 2026, Gracenote (Nielsen's content-intelligence business) and PubMatic announced a partnership whose implementation runs on the IAB Tech Lab's ARTF and is built to operate within PubMatic's AgenticOS.
s: Nielsen/Gracenote, nielsen.com news-center, 2026-06-17; PR Newswire, 2026-06-17; Storyboard18, 2026-06-18. Accessed 2026-06-20. Tier 1 company release + Tier 5 trade.

claims.t: The integration matches bid opportunities against Gracenote episode-level data in real time at-auction, 'adding just 0.1 to 0.5 milliseconds to transactions.
s: Nielsen/PR Newswire, 2026-06-17 (accessed 2026-06-20); comparators from corpus docs 04 §1.3, 06. Tier 1 company claim.

claims.t: Gracenote occupies a tenant category absent from doc 04's participant taxonomy, which lists only a full DSP (Bedrock), AI-decisioning vendors, buyer-side intelligence (MiQ), and agencies — not a contextual/content-metadata vendor.
s: Nielsen/PR Newswire 2026-06-17; Storyboard18 2026-06-18; corpus doc 04 §1.1, §3.3. Tier 1 + Tier 5 vs. corpus.

claims.t: Contextual-data vendors fit the containerized model more naturally than the bidders the corpus foregrounds, because they hold exactly the show-level data doc 03 §2.3 says CTV sellers refuse to put in the open bidstream — the container computes the match in-cell and returns only the result.
s: Corpus doc 03 §2.3; PPC Land on the Gracenote survey, 2026-05-14 (accessed 2026-06-20). Tier 5 + corpus inference.

claims.t: The Index Exchange–Gracenote integration (industry-first SSP integration of Gracenote, Sept 16 2025; show-level reporting with Spectrum Reach at CES, Jan 7 2026) is a conventional reporting/data integration, not containerized and not on ARTF.
s: Gracenote newsroom 2025-09-16; Index Exchange/Nielsen 2026-01-07; thedesk.net 2026-01 (all accessed 2026-06-20). Tier 1 + Tier 5.

claims.t: Peer39, IRIS.TV, and Comscore all supply program-level contextual CTV data and are the natural peer cohort, but none is documented running on ARTF or in a containerized SSP fabric in this window; only Gracenote-on-PubMatic is a confirmed containerized contextual tenant.
s: Peer39 product page; IRIS.TV/Beet.TV materials; PubMatic–IRIS.TV blog 2025-05-27; Comscore release 2026-01-06 (all accessed 2026-06-20). Tier 1 vendor + Tier 5 trade.

claims.t: As of June 20, 2026 the Gracenote–PubMatic ARTF integration is announced and presented as operational but carries no independent production-scale audit; PubMatic asserts 'tens of millions of verified live sports impressions' and no release uses 'beta/pilot' language.
s: Nielsen/PR Newswire 2026-06-17 (accessed 2026-06-20), cross-checked vs. corpus doc 04 evidence note. Tier 1 company claim.

claims.t: On Feb 26, 2026 WPP announced Elevate28, transitioning from a holding-company structure to a single integrated company with four AI-enabled units (WPP Media, WPP Creative, WPP Production, WPP Enterprise Solutions) built on WPP Open, targeting GBP 500M savings by 2028.
s: WPP plc, Elevate28 Strategy Update, wpp.com, Feb 26, 2026; Marketing Dive, Feb 2026.

claims.t: On Jun 18, 2026 WPP Media launched an Agentic Standards Initiative and Buyer Agent for Video inside WPP Open's orchestration layer, a buyer-agent/seller-agent negotiation topology, a different architecture from running a proprietary bidder inside an SSP's compute fabric.
s: WPP Media, Establishing trusted standards for agentic video buying, Jun 18, 2026; LBBOnline; Storyboard18.

claims.t: As of mid-2026 none of WPP Media, Omnicom (post-IPG), or Publicis has deployed a proprietary bidder inside Index Cloud, Decision Fabric, or OpenXBuild; all build the layer above the fabric (orchestration, principal media, identity) rather than becoming tenants.
s: Synthesis across Index Exchange (Apr 2026), PPC Land Bedrock, AdExchanger GroupM/PubMatic (May 2025), WPP Media (Jun 2026), Digiday Omnicom-IPG (2025).

claims.t: GroupM/WPP Media's most recent detailed SSP posture is partnership-based curation (PubMatic Connect, the Premium Marketplace) and aligning its buying to SSP RTB, a federated model that explicitly does NOT run its own models inside the exchange.
s: AdExchanger, How GroupM Is Collaborating With PubMatic As The SSP Gets Closer To The Buy Side, May 22, 2025.

claims.t: Omnicom closed IPG on Nov 26, 2025, becoming the largest holdco by revenue; its thesis is scale-as-AI-training-data (Omni + Acxiom + Flywheel) plus a fast-growing principal-media book (est. 2B-dollar-plus in 2025), a rival closer-to-supply move distinct from co-locating a bidder.
s: Omnicom/SEC, IPG close Nov 26, 2025; Digiday Omnicom-IPG, 2025; AdExchanger, The Rise Of Principal Media, Mar 18, 2026.

claims.t: Publicis pursues the data route, Epsilon plus Lotame (Mar 2025, ~1.6B IDs toward a ~4B-profile graph) plus AdgeAI plus a pending 2.2B-dollar LiveRamp deal, assembling the identity layer a containerized model must consume, positioning data as the choke point over the fabric.
s: VideoWeek (Mar 2025); Publicis Groupe release (Mar 2025); LiveRamp SEC DEFA14A/8-K FY2026; The Drum, 2026.

claims.t: Containerized bidding is a real in-housing accelerant, letting advertisers run proprietary models against live supply without DSP infrastructure (Hyundai own that) against an established trend (ANA 82% in-house; 35% expanded in-house programmatic; 60% spend less due to AI), but the net threat to the agency layer is indeterminate because holdcos aim to supply the in-housing platform/identity/orchestration.
s: AdExchanger Hyundai, Jun 16, 2026; eMarketer agency/AI FAQs, 2026; Ad Age/ANA in-house programmatic.

claims.t: Independents and holdcos play different games: independents rent the container for supply access without infrastructure, while holdcos decline tenancy and shape the standard from above, because going in would relocate their decisioning brain into a supply-side landlord's data center and surrender leverage.
s: Index Exchange (Apr 2026); PPC Land Bedrock; AdExchanger Goodway; Adweek ARTF roster; Digiday, Agencies are moving closer to supply, May 20, 2026.

claims.t: Both Omnicom and Publicis ran formal audits of The Trade Desk's fee structures in 2026, scrutinizing the DSP layer even as they build agentic/identity layers that could absorb its function; TTD's counter is expanding direct-to-brand relationships to route around holdco gatekeepers.
s: Marketing Brew, How The Trade Desk is aiming to remain king of the open web, Apr 9, 2026.

claims.t: Co-locating the bidder inside the exchange collapses cloud-egress cost: an AWS worked example (AWS for Industries, Jun 16 2026) shows a DSP's monthly networking bill dropping ~84% (from ~$13,666 to ~$2,192) and an SSP's ~65% (from ~$29,663 to ~$10,532) on a workload of ~8.64 billion requests/day (~259 billion/month), 3KB/bid, ~725 TB/month.
s: AWS for Industries blog, 'Next-generation programmatic advertising: How AWS RTB Fabric redefines the game,' 2026-06-16.

claims.t: AWS RTB Fabric — a managed-network service for real-time-bidding workloads (NOT in-exchange container co-location; it optimizes the round-trip rather than eliminating it) — reached GA Oct 23 2025 advertising 'up to 80% lower networking costs,' single-digit-millisecond latency, across six regions; it is the hyperscaler's adjacent answer to the same latency/egress problem containerization attacks.
s: AWS, 'Now generally available: AWS RTB Fabric for real-time bidding workloads,' What's New, 2025-10-23.

claims.t: The headline 'up to 80%' networking-cost saving is measured against cloud LIST pricing; against a buyer's already-negotiated hyperscale contract the realized saving is only ~20-25% (TripleLift's own figure) — the load-bearing caveat for ROI modeling.
s: AdExchanger, 'AWS Launches A Cloud Infrastructure Service For Ad Tech,' 2025-10-23.

claims.t: inPowered AI's model running inside Index Exchange (sell-side decisioning) drove a 75% reduction in cost per site visit for a major apparel retailer in online video (Index case study, Feb 3 2026) — but it is a vendor-run case study with no disclosed holdout/control and no MRC accreditation.
s: Index Exchange, 'How Sell-Side Decisioning Drove a 75% Drop in Cost per Visit,' case study, 2026-02-03.

claims.t: As of June 2026 NO MRC accreditation exists for containerized-bidder / sell-side-decisioning PERFORMANCE LIFT; the MRC's Digital Advertising Auction Transparency Standards (finalized Jan 2026) govern auction DISCLOSURE, are voluntary, and do not validate lift.
s: MRC, 'Digital Advertising Auction Transparency Standards,' final, January 2026; corroborated by trade coverage.

claims.t: The broader performance-lift cluster (5x-16x ROAS, 50-80% CPA reductions from custom-bidding vendors) is entirely vendor-run holdouts or self-reported case studies, none independently replicated or MRC-accredited.
s: Synthesis of vendor case studies + PPC Land / trade coverage; see doc 05 sources [5][9].

claims.t: ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark Q3 2025: working media on web and mobile rose from 36% (2023) to 47.1% (Q3 2025) — ~$13.6B recovered efficiency in a ~$123B market — meaning ~53% of the advertiser dollar still does NOT reach the publisher on web/mobile.
s: ANA, 'Programmatic Transparency Benchmark: Q3 2025,' November 2025.

claims.t: ANA Q3 2025, CTV: seller (publisher) revenue rose from 74.8% to 76.2% of total ad spend, driven mainly by a ~1.9-point drop in SSP fees (14.7% -> 12.8%); ~24% of the CTV dollar is still consumed before the publisher.
s: ANA, 'Programmatic Transparency Benchmark: Q3 2025,' November 2025.

claims.t: DSP take-rates: The Trade Desk ~20% (~20.3% in 2024; 19-21% range); independent DSPs typically 10-15%; Amazon DSP ~1% on open-web inventory (0% on Amazon-owned media).
s: TTD investor materials; Adage/eMarketer DSP-fee coverage, 2025.

claims.t: In 2025 Google, Amazon, and The Trade Desk all moved on DSP fees; Amazon DSP's ~1% open-web take (vs Google's ~4% on programmatic-guaranteed) pressured TTD's once-'fixed' 15-20% fees into being negotiable, with 1-2% reductions or post-auction discounts for agencies hitting spend thresholds.
s: Adage / eMarketer / Digiday, 2025.

claims.t: Adalytics log-level research: combined DSP+SSP fees 'up to ~35% on average'; median single-SSP supply fee ~20%; extreme cases where platforms retain ~98% (publisher ~2%); ISBA 2020 baseline ~51% of advertiser spend reached the publisher.
s: Adalytics, 'How much in fees are ad tech companies charging?'; ISBA 2020 Programmatic Supply Chain Transparency Study.

claims.t: As of June 2026 no containerized-bidding fabric operator (Index Exchange, PubMatic, Magnite) has published a price card; every 'who pays whom' model (hosting fee, revenue-share on lift, stacked take-rate, CPM premium, exclusivity premium) is structured inference, not disclosed fact.
s: Index Exchange + PubMatic launch materials, 2026; ExchangeWire, 2026-06-17.

claims.t: Bedrock Platform is positioned as a new 'direct DSP' / 'Direct Booking Engine' competing on 'dramatically lower take rates' and sitting closer to supply, though no specific take-rate percentage is published.
s: ExchangeWire, 'A New Type of DSP Is Emerging,' 2026-06-17.
