s: Apple Advertising Policies (2025-02-26); Campaigns & Elections 2025-02-21; AdWave 2026-04-07; Amazon Ads prohibited-content policy; multiple 2026 Netflix-ad trade reports. Accessed 2026-06-23.

claims.t: Within Disney, Hulu accepts candidate and issue political ads (aligned to Disney general-entertainment/ESPN policy after its July 2022 reversal) while Disney+ continues to refuse, and this split is intact in the 2026 cycle.

claims.t: YouTube and YouTube TV (Google) accept U.S. political/election advertising in 2026, gated by Google's Election Ads verification (identity/location checks, 'Paid for by' disclosure) and subject to limits on targeting by sensitive attributes.

claims.t: Samsung Ads and LG Ad Solutions maintain dedicated 2026 political-ad offerings pitching ACR-driven voter targeting on their own inventory; Vizio (Walmart) is grouped among OEM platforms accepting political inventory.

claims.t: Roku, Peacock (NBCUniversal), Tubi (Fox), and Paramount+/Pluto TV all accept political advertising in the 2026 cycle, each via a verified-political-entity process with creative review.

claims.t: Ted Sarandos's February 3, 2026 Senate appearance was a Judiciary antitrust-subcommittee hearing on Netflix's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery; political advertising did not come up, so the testimony does not bear on Netflix's political-ad policy and the corpus's implied link should be cut.

claims.t: Peirce credited Alexander Bain's definition of belief — 'that upon which a man is prepared to act' — as the foundational insight behind the pragmatic maxim, transmitted through Nicholas St. John Green.
s: Peirce, Writings vol. 3 (T1)

claims.t: The Cambridge Metaphysical Club's historical record rests primarily on Peirce's retrospective manuscript written ~30 years later; contemporary corroboration from Holmes Papers and James correspondence is not systematically established.

Peirce retrospective (T1)

claims.t: Peirce's pragmatic maxim (1878): 'Consider what effects, which might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object.' The maxim is modal, not consequentialist.
s: Peirce, How to Make Our Ideas Clear (1878), Writings vol. 3 (T1)

claims.t: Peirce defined truth as 'the opinion fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate' — a convergence theory identifying the real as the object of that ultimate opinion.
s: Peirce, How to Make Our Ideas Clear (T1)
Essential Peirce vol. 1 (T1)

claims.t: James's pragmatic theory of truth holds that true ideas are those we can validate, corroborate, and verify across the full downstream of experience — not 'whatever is convenient to believe.' The caricature misrepresents a theory with stringent downstream constraints.
s: James, Pragmatism (1907) (T1)
James, Meaning of Truth (1909) (T1)
Lovejoy, Thirteen Pragmatisms (1908) as contestation (T2)

claims.t: Misak's New Pragmatism rehabilitates Peirce's convergence theory against Rorty: truth is what would survive indefinite critical inquiry, providing a genuine norm beyond solidarity that every sincere assertor is already committed to.
s: Misak, Truth and the End of Inquiry (T2)
Misak, New Pragmatists (T2)

claims.t: Rorty's Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979) argued that the mind-as-mirror-of-nature picture underlies all traditional epistemology and that abandoning it dissolves rather than solves traditional philosophical problems.
s: Rorty, Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979) (T1)

claims.t: Horkheimer's Eclipse of Reason (1947) argues that pragmatism reduces reason to its instrumental function; this critique lands hardest on Dewey's middle period but has not been fully answered. The strongest Deweyan reply distinguishes intelligent guidance of ends from mere efficiency.
s: Horkheimer, Eclipse of Reason (1947) (T1)

claims.t: The Davidson-Rorty debate is the clearest case study for distinguishing Peircean from Rortyan pragmatism: both reject representationalism, but Davidson's insistence that truth is primitive and irreducible marks the fault line that defines the contemporary split.
s: Davidson and Rorty primary texts (T1)
Misak (T2)

claims.t: On the dominant scholarly reading (Sanders, Meier, Fredriksen), the historical Jesus was a first-century Jewish apocalyptic prophet who proclaimed the imminent reign of God and did not set out to found an institution.
s: E.P. Sanders, The Historical Figure of Jesus (1993); Paula Fredriksen, From Jesus to Christ (1988); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The institutional, hierarchically governed church is a development of the decades and centuries after Jesus, driven by resurrection belief and the delay of the Kingdom, not a turnkey founding by the historical Jesus.
s: Ehrman, 'Who Founded the Catholic Church?'; Fredriksen (1988); U.S. Catholic, 'How did Jesus found the church?'; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The three Petrine texts give Peter singular NT prominence; the 'rock' of Matthew 16:18 (Petros/petra; Aramaic kepha) is most naturally Peter himself, a reading on which many Evangelical and Orthodox exegetes have converged, conceding the Petrine point while leaving the Roman point open.
s: NRSVCE via BibleGateway; Jimmy Akin, 'The Petrine Fact' (position-evidence); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The 1973 ecumenical study Peter in the New Testament (Brown, Donfried, Reumann) established the 'Petrine trajectory': the NT presents not a static office but a developing image of Peter that grows across its writings.
s: Brown, Donfried, Reumann (eds.), Peter in the New Testament (Augsburg/Paulist, 1973); Ministry Magazine summary 1974; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Jesuit church historian Klaus Schatz, in the standard scholarly history Papal Primacy, states that 'Roman primacy was not a given from the outset' but underwent a long development whose initial phases extended into the fifth century — a Catholic-historian concession of the development thesis.
s: Klaus Schatz, S.J., Papal Primacy: From Its Origins to the Present (Liturgical Press, 1996; Ger. 1990); litpress.org; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Roman claims to settle disputes for other churches were repeatedly resisted in the 2nd-3rd centuries: Irenaeus and others rebuked Pope Victor I's attempted excommunication of the Quartodecimans (c.190s), and Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea flatly resisted Pope Stephen I's claim (grounded in Petrine succession) to settle the rebaptism question (c.255-257).
s: OCA, 'The Quartodeciman Controversy'; 'Cyprian vs. Stephen'; Catholic Encyclopedia 'The Pope' (position-evidence across spectrum); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Eastern church theorized primacy as a function of a city's imperial importance: Constantinople canon 3 (381) ranked Constantinople second 'after Rome, because Constantinople is New Rome,' and Chalcedon canon 28 (451) granted it privileges equal to Rome's on the same principle — a primacy theology fundamentally different from Rome's apostolic-Petrine theory.
s: Constantinople I canon 3 (Early Church Texts); Chalcedon canon 28; Britannica; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Pope Gregory the Great (c.595) denounced anyone calling himself 'universal bishop' as a 'precursor of the Antichrist' (objecting to the Constantinopolitan patriarch's title) and styled himself 'servant of the servants of God' — a Roman pope repudiating the title of universal supremacy.
s: Britannica, 'St. Gregory the Great'; Christian History Institute, 'Precursor of Antichrist'; R.A. Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Ignatius of Antioch (c.107-117) is the charter witness for a single bishop ruling above the presbyters, but he is prescribing/promoting the model rather than describing a settled universal fact, has no developed doctrine of apostolic succession, and notably does not mention a single bishop of Rome — consistent with Rome's still being governed by a presbyterial college at that date.
s: Ignatius, Epistles; Allen Brent via Project MUSE; Schatz, Papal Primacy; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Irenaeus (Against Heresies, c.180) developed apostolic succession as a standard of orthodoxy against the Gnostics, using bishop-lists (Rome's as paradigm) and the 'rule of faith'; his phrase for Rome (potentior principalitas) is among the most contested in the early-papacy literature, with translations ranging from 'preeminent authority' to claims only about Rome's convenience as a meeting-point.
s: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III; Cambridge History of Christianity, Vol. 1 (Mitchell & Young, eds.); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Roman persecution of Christians was real but episodic (concentrated under Nero locally, Decius 250, Valerian 257-260, Diocletian 303-311), not a continuous three-century campaign; Candida Moss argues the 'Age of Martyrs' as sustained persecution is largely a later construction and many martyr-acts are embellished, while the cult and narrative of martyrdom were enormously consequential regardless of raw numbers.
s: W.H.C. Frend, The Rise of Christianity; Candida Moss, The Myth of Persecution (HarperOne, 2013); Cambridge History of Christianity Vol. 1; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The NT canon formed gradually (2nd-4th c.), catalyzed by Marcion's truncated canon (c.140); the Muratorian Fragment (c.170-200) already names most eventual books, and the fixed 27 are first listed in Athanasius's Festal Letter of 367 and ratified at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) — showing Scripture and Tradition emerged together, the canon a product of the church's tradition.
s: Bruce Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford, 1987); 'Development of the NT canon' (map to cited sources); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The 'Edict of Milan' (313) granted toleration and restored confiscated property — it did NOT make Christianity the state religion (that came under Theodosius, 380-392) — but Constantine's patronage (clergy privileges, the Lateran, the basilicas) transformed the church into a wealthy, publicly recognized, property-owning body and inserted the emperor as convener and enforcer of councils.
s: Britannica, 'Edict of Milan' and 'Constantine I'; T.D. Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981); H.A. Drake, Constantine and the Bishops (2000); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Nicaea (325) declared the Son homoousios ('of the same substance') with the Father against Arius, but did NOT end the controversy; per Ayres and Hanson, 'pro-Nicene' Trinitarian theology as later understood did not exist in 325 and was a late-4th-century achievement (360s-380s) of Athanasius and the Cappadocians, who stabilized the 'one ousia, three hypostaseis' grammar — orthodoxy's victory was contingent and nearly reversed under Constantius II.
s: Lewis Ayres, Nicaea and Its Legacy (OUP, 2004); R.P.C. Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988); Britannica; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Ephesus (431) affirmed Mary as Theotokos and condemned Nestorius, separating the Church of the East; Chalcedon (451) defined one person in two natures, separating the miaphysite Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian) — the first permanent rupture of the imperial church; modern dialogue judges the Chalcedonian split substantially terminological.
s: Councils of Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) acts; Britannica; Leo's Tome (EWTN); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Leo I (440-461) articulated the mature Petrine theory of the Roman bishop as Peter's heir/vicar; his Tome shaped Chalcedon ('Peter has spoken through Leo'), and he rejected Chalcedon's canon 28 outright, insisting ecclesiastical rank follows apostolic foundation rather than imperial dignity — the Roman counter-principle in its purest form.
s: Leo's Tome (EWTN); Schatz, Papal Primacy; Chalcedon analyses; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Pope Gelasius I (c.494) supplied the West's enduring political theology in the 'two powers' doctrine — the sacred auctoritas of priests and the royal potestas of kings, with priestly authority the weightier in spiritual matters — seeding the entire medieval papacy-empire contest.
s: Gelasius I, Letter to Anastasius (c.494); ODCC, 'Gelasius I'; accessed 2026-06-25 (from the scholarly record)

claims.t: Augustine of Hippo (354-430) gave the Latin West its distinctive theology: against the Donatists, sacramental efficacy independent of the minister's holiness (later ex opere operato) and the Church as a 'mixed body'; against the Pelagians, original sin, the bondage of the will, and the priority of grace; and in City of God a two-cities theology of history — divergences with no exact Eastern counterpart that feed the eventual estrangement.
s: Augustine, City of God and anti-Pelagian/anti-Donatist works; Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967); SEP; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Jerome (c.347-420) produced the Vulgate, the Latin Bible that was the standard text of Western Christianity for over a millennium (and was made authoritative at Trent); Ambrose of Milan (c.339-397) asserted episcopal authority over imperial power, compelling Theodosius I to do public penance after the 390 Thessalonica massacre — prefiguring the medieval claim of spiritual authority over rulers.
s: Jerome, Vulgate; EBSCO 'Saint Jerome'; Ambrose, Letters; ODCC; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: By the eve of 1054 East and West had drifted into estrangement along multiple axes (language, two rival theories of primacy, the filioque addition which the East rejected as an unauthorized creedal alteration, and the political fracture of Charlemagne's 800 coronation); Chadwick shows Rome itself resisted inserting filioque to c.800, and the Photian schism (860s) foreshadowed 1054, making the mutual excommunications of 1054 a symptom rather than a cause.
s: Henry Chadwick, East and West (OUP, 2003); Filioque scholarship; accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The churches that broke from the imperial church at Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) survive as living institutions today: the Oriental Orthodox communion (Coptic, Armenian Apostolic, Syriac, Ethiopian, and others) numbers roughly 60 million members worldwide, and the Assyrian Church of the East about 400,000 (Iraq, Iran, Syria, Lebanon, North America, Australia), still active as of 2026.
s: Oriental Orthodox Churches and Assyrian Church of the East reference profiles (membership estimates); ACE news (2026-02 meeting); accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The mutual excommunications of 1054 (Cardinal Humbert vs. Patriarch Michael Cerularius) were personal and limited, not a formal break between the Eastern and Western churches; the scholarly consensus treats 1054 as a symbolic marker terminating a centuries-long estrangement rather than as the operative cause of schism.
s: Britannica, 'East-West Schism' and 'Christianity — The Photian schism and the great East-West schism,' accessed 2026-06-25, britannica.com

claims.t: The Latin sack of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in April 1204 turned the slow Catholic-Orthodox estrangement into a deep and lasting wound, and is better dated than 1054 as the decisive sealing event of the schism.
s: Britannica, 'Sack of Constantinople (1204),' accessed 2026-06-25, britannica.com/event/Sack-of-Constantinople-1204

claims.t: The filioque dispute concerns the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit: the Latin West (following Augustine) inserted 'and the Son' into the Nicene Creed, while the Greek East (articulated by Photius in the 860s) held the Spirit proceeds 'from the Father alone,' allowing 'through the Son' only for the Spirit's temporal mission.
s: Britannica, 'Christianity — The Photian schism,' accessed 2026-06-25, britannica.com/topic/Christianity/The-Photian-schism-and-the-great-East-West-schism

claims.t: The decisive East-West dispute was over papal primacy: Rome claimed a primacy of jurisdiction (real monarchical authority over the patriarchs) while the East granted only a primacy of honor within the pentarchy of five ancient patriarchates.
s: Britannica, 'East-West Schism,' accessed 2026-06-25; Vatican News, 'lifting of the anathemas, sixty years on,' 2026-01

claims.t: On 7 December 1965, Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I jointly removed the 1054 anathemas from memory in a Common Declaration read simultaneously in Rome and Istanbul; the gesture expressed reconciliation but did not end the schism.
s: Common Declaration of Paul VI and Athenagoras I, 7 Dec 1965, vatican.va; Vatican News, 2026-01

claims.t: The Gregorian Reform (c. 1050–1080, associated with Gregory VII) sought to restore libertas ecclesiae — the Church's freedom from lay control — by ending simony and clerical concubinage and barring lay investiture of bishops.
s: Britannica, 'Investiture Controversy' and 'St. Gregory VII — Papal Reforms,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: At Canossa in January 1077, Henry IV did public penance before Gregory VII to obtain absolution from excommunication, and by submitting implicitly conceded the pope's right to depose secular monarchs — though the wider Investiture Controversy was not settled until the Concordat of Worms (1122).
s: Britannica, 'Investiture Controversy,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Pope Innocent III (r. 1198–1216) developed papal monarchy to its medieval zenith, claiming supremacy over Europe's kings under the doctrine of plenitudo potestatis (fullness of power), and convened the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), which gave the term transubstantiation its first conciliar use.
s: New World Encyclopedia, 'Innocent III'; Encyclopedia.com, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Boniface VIII's bull Unam Sanctam (18 November 1302) made the most extreme assertion of papal supremacy — declaring subjection to the Roman pontiff 'altogether necessary to salvation' — yet asserted no authority not already claimed by Gregory VII; he was answered by the Outrage of Anagni (7 September 1303), when Philip IV's agent Nogaret seized the pope, who died weeks later.
s: Unam Sanctam (Boniface VIII, 1302), primary text; Schaff, History of the Christian Church vol. 6, ccel.org

claims.t: Scholasticism was a method that harmonized faith and reason and reconciled Christian theology with Aristotle, running from Anselm's fides quaerens intellectum through Abelard's dialectic to its crown in Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (composed c. 1265–74), which held faith and reason to be distinct but harmonious domains.
s: New World Encyclopedia, 'Scholasticism'; Wikipedia 'Scholasticism' (navigation), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Aquinas's Five Ways (quinque viae) at Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3 are five arguments for God's existence from natural reason alone — drawn from motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and final order — exemplifying his conviction that natural reason can demonstrate God's existence.
s: Britannica, 'the Five Ways'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Paris bishop Étienne Tempier issued the Condemnation of 1277 (219 propositions banned as heretical), aimed at Latin Averroist Aristotelianism but catching some theses associated with Aquinas; the Duhem thesis influentially argues it loosened Aristotelian necessity and encouraged later scientific questioning, a contested claim.
s: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Condemnation of 1277,' accessed 2026-06-25, plato.stanford.edu/entries/condemnation/

claims.t: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) led the late-medieval nominalist via moderna — denying real existence to universals and emphasizing God's absolute power — which dominated the universities (including Erfurt, where Luther was trained) and loosened the Thomist bond of faith and reason.
s: New World Encyclopedia / Wikipedia 'Scholasticism' (navigation), accessed 2026-06-25; Erfurt-Luther link is author synthesis

claims.t: Religious renewal proceeded in waves — Cluny (founded 909/910), the Cistercians at Cîteaux (1098), and then the genuinely new thirteenth-century mendicant orders (Franciscans under Francis c. 1181–1226; Dominicans under Dominic c. 1170–1221) who abandoned monastic stability to beg, preach, and educate in the new cities.
s: Benedict XVI, General Audience 13 Jan 2010, vatican.va; Medievalists.net (2025); Schaff, History of the Christian Church vol. 5

claims.t: From 1309 to 1377 seven successive French popes resided at Avignon under French royal influence, until Gregory XI returned the papacy to Rome in January 1377.
s: Britannica, 'Western Schism'; Lumen Learning Western Civilization, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Western Schism (1378–1417) began with a disputed 1378 double election (Urban VI in Rome, Clement VII in Avignon), and the Council of Pisa (1409) produced a third claimant, leaving three rival papacies until the Council of Constance restored unity under Martin V in 1417.
s: Britannica, 'Western Schism'; Lumen Learning, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Council of Constance proclaimed conciliarism — that a general council holds authority over the pope (decree Haec Sancta, 1415) — but the doctrine did not survive in practice: later popes reasserted papal supremacy, the Council of Basel (1431–49) discredited the movement, and by the mid-1400s it had stalled; whether Haec Sancta was a binding dogmatic decree remains disputed.
s: Lumen Learning, 'The Western Schism,' accessed 2026-06-25; Haec Sancta status analysis is author synthesis

claims.t: Late-medieval reforming critics anticipated the Reformation: John Wyclif (c. 1328–1384) held the Bible over the Church and inspired the Lollards and an English vernacular Bible; Jan Hus, taking up Wyclif's ideas, was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415 despite a safe conduct.
s: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Wyclif'; general Constance accounts, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses against indulgences crystallized into three principles defining Protestantism — justification by faith alone (sola fide, with imputed not infused righteousness), Scripture alone (sola scriptura), and the priesthood of all believers — leading to his excommunication in 1521 after he burned the bull Exsurge Domine.
s: Christian Publishing House (2025); Southern Equip / SBTS, accessed 2026-06-25 (Protestant lean, used for descriptive content)

claims.t: The Reformation fractured early: Zwingli rejected transubstantiation and split from Luther over the Eucharist at the Marburg Colloquy (October 1529); Calvin systematized Reformed theology in the Institutes (1536), taught predestination, and made Geneva the leading Protestant center with a seminary training reformers for Europe.
s: Study.com, 'Ulrich Zwingli & John Calvin'; Wikipedia 'John Calvin' (navigation), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Henry VIII's break with Rome via the Act of Supremacy of 1534 was initially political — driven by his desired annulment from Catherine of Aragon — and established a Church under royal headship that initially retained much Catholic doctrine and liturgy.
s: Christianity in the modern era' overview / Study.com, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Council of Trent met in three discontinuous periods — 1545–47 (Paul III, 13 sessions), 1551–52 (Julius III, 6 sessions), and 1562–63 (Pius IV, 6 sessions, peak ~280 bishops) — working simultaneously on doctrinal definition and disciplinary reform.
s: St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, 'The Council of Trent,' accessed 2026-06-25, saet.ac.uk/Christianity/CouncilofTrent

claims.t: Trent's Decree on Justification (Session 6, 13 January 1547) rejected sola fide and imputed righteousness, teaching justification as both forgiveness and real interior renewal requiring free consent and good works that earn further merit; it was a Thomist-Scotist compromise that also rejected Seripando's double-justification theory.
s: St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, 'The Council of Trent,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Trent's Session 4 (8 April 1546) taught a single source of revelation (the gospel) transmitted through two channels — Scripture and apostolic tradition — defending Tradition against sola scriptura; the hardened 'two sources' doctrine often attributed to Trent was a later systematization, not the council's own teaching. The same session fixed the canon (including the deuterocanonical books) and declared the Vulgate authentic.
s: St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, 'The Council of Trent,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Trent reaffirmed all seven sacraments against Lutheran reduction to two (Session 7, 3 March 1547) and defined the Eucharistic change as transubstantiation (Session 13, 11 October 1551), the conversion of the substance of bread and wine into Christ's body and blood, diverging from Lutheran consubstantiation.
s: St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, 'The Council of Trent,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Trent's disciplinary revolution required bishops to reside in their dioceses (declared a divinum praeceptum, divine precept, Session 23, 15 July 1563) and mandated a diocesan seminary in every diocese to train candidates for the priesthood — the institution that produced the educated, celibate parish clergy of modern Catholicism.
s: St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, 'The Council of Trent,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The historiographical dispute over whether Trent was 'reform' or 'reaction' turns on terminology — 'Counter-Reformation' (reaction) vs. 'Catholic Reformation' (internal renewal) vs. John O'Malley's neutral 'early modern Catholicism' — and the current scholarly consensus, building on Jedin, Evennett, Delumeau, Schilling, Bireley, and O'Malley, increasingly judges the dichotomy false: Trent was visibly both.
s: Oxford Bibliographies, 'Catholic/Counter-Reformation'; O'Malley, Trent and All That (Harvard, 2000); St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola and approved in 1540, remains a living institution and is, per the Annuario Pontificio 2026 / Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae 2024, the largest men's religious order in the Catholic Church, with about 18,711 members worldwide.
s: Vatican News, 'New data of Annuario Pontificio 2026,' 2026-03; gcatholic.org, 'Religious Orders for Men with most members,' accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Sixteenth-century Catholicism became a global religion carried on Spanish and Portuguese ships, with Jesuit accommodation in Asia (Francis Xavier d. 1552; Matteo Ricci in China 1552–1610) and entanglement with imperial coercion in the Americas; the Church's conscience split, producing the papal bull Sublimis Deus (1537) affirming indigenous rationality, the New Laws (1542), and the Valladolid debate (1550–51) between Las Casas and Sepúlveda, which the judges left unresolved.
s: Britannica, 'Roman Catholic mission, 1500–1950'; History Today, 'The Valladolid Debate'; Cambridge Handbook of Human Dignity, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Society of Jesus with the brief Dominus ac Redemptor on 21 July 1773 under pressure from the Catholic Bourbon courts, and the order was universally restored by Pius VII via Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum on 7 August 1814.
s: Boston College Jesuit Portal, Dominus ac Redemptor (1773); Jesuits Global, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790) subordinated the French Church to the state and split the clergy, with only about seven bishops and roughly half of parish priests taking the loyalty oath (jurors vs. non-jurors).
s: Britannica, 'Civil Constitution of the Clergy'; World History Encyclopedia, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The dechristianization campaign of September 1793 to July 1794 closed churches, persecuted clergy, and promoted civic cults; estimates place clergy and religious killed at roughly 2,000 directly and higher when provincial mass executions (Nantes noyades, Lyon) are included.
s: Reference accounts (dechristianization of France); Institute of World Politics, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 25 February 1803, under French/Russian pressure, secularized roughly 70 ecclesiastical principalities (including the prince-archbishoprics of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne), dissolving the German Church's territorial sovereignties.
s: Reference accounts, 'Reichsdeputationshauptschluss' and 'Secularization (church property),' accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Nineteenth-century ultramontanism centralized Catholic authority on the papacy as the one stable post-Revolutionary source of authority, defeating Gallicanism, Febronianism, and Josephinism; Joseph de Maistre's Du Pape (1819) gave it its founding argument for papal supremacy in church and state.
s: Britannica, 'Ultramontanism'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Ultramontanism,' accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Pius IX issued the Syllabus of Errors in 1864 (appended to Quanta Cura), condemning eighty propositions of liberal modernity, the last rejecting that the pope should reconcile with 'progress, liberalism, and modern civilization.
s: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Pius IX Issues the Syllabus of Errors'; Britannica, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The First Vatican Council (opened 8 Dec 1869) defined papal infallibility and universal jurisdiction in Pastor Aeternus (18 July 1870); infallibility is bounded to ex cathedra definitions of faith and morals, the decisive 13 July vote was 451-88-62, and the council was suspended on 20 Sep 1870 when Italian troops took Rome.
s: Pastor Aeternus (1870), primary; Britannica, 'First Vatican Council'; reference accounts, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Vatican I's infallibility definition was contested: Ignaz von Doellinger rejected it as resting on 'forgeries and distortions of history' (excommunicated 1871, seeding the Old Catholic schism), while John Henry Newman, who opposed defining it as dogma but accepted the narrow result, judged the minimalist definition a defeat for the maximal ultramontanes.
s: America Magazine, 'The man who fought papal infallibility' (2017); EWTN, 'Newman on Councils,' accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The 1870 loss of Rome opened the Roman Question; popes refused the 1871 Law of Guarantees and styled themselves 'prisoners in the Vatican' until the Lateran Pacts (signed 11 Feb 1929, ratified 7 June 1929) created sovereign Vatican City State, recognized the Holy See's independence, and compensated it financially.
s: Britannica, 'Roman question'; EBSCO, 'Lateran Treaty'; Lateran Treaty text (uniset.ca), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum Novarum (15 May 1891) founded modern Catholic social teaching, defending private property against socialism while affirming the dignity of labor, a living wage, the right of workers to organize, and a role for the state, and rejecting both socialism and laissez-faire capitalism.
s: Rerum Novarum (1891), primary; Britannica, 'Rerum Novarum,' accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Under Pius X the Church condemned 'Modernism' via Lamentabili (1907, 65 propositions) and Pascendi Dominici Gregis (1907, 'the synthesis of all heresies'), imposed the anti-Modernist oath in 1910 (abolished by Paul VI in 1967), and excommunicated its chief targets, Alfred Loisy (1908) and George Tyrrell (1907).
s: Britannica, 'Pascendi Dominici Gregis'; Modernism reference accounts, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The conduct of Pius XII during the Holocaust is genuinely contested: critics (Hochhuth's The Deputy 1963, Cornwell's Hitler's Pope 1999, Kertzer's archival work) charge culpable silence despite knowledge by autumn 1942, while defenders cite calculated prudence to avoid reprisals, ~55 prewar protests, Mit Brennender Sorge drafting, and convent rescues; the 2020 archive opening has complicated rather than settled it.
s: Benedictine College Media & Culture; Yad Vashem (Gorsky); Smithsonian, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Pope Francis opened the Pius XII archives on 2 March 2020 after a 14-year inventory; early sensational claims by historians including Hubert Wolf were criticized by other scholars as overstated, and the documentary base is still being worked through.
s: NPR, 'Vatican Opens Archives Of World War II-Era Pope Pius XII' (2 Mar 2020); Times of Israel (2020), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The Second Vatican Council met 11 Oct 1962 to 8 Dec 1965 under John XXIII and Paul VI under the watchword aggiornamento, drew 2,000-2,500 bishops plus ~460 periti (women present only as observers), and produced sixteen documents including the constitutions Lumen Gentium, Dei Verbum, and Sacrosanctum Concilium and the declarations Nostra Aetate and Dignitatis Humanae.
s: Britannica, 'Second Vatican Council'; USCCB; Vatican.va council index, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Lumen Gentium (1964) reframed the Church as mystery, communion, and 'People of God' called to holiness, and articulated collegiality - the bishops, together with and never without the pope, sharing in the governance of the universal Church - as the conciliar counterweight to Vatican I's centralization.
s: Lumen Gentium (1964), primary; Britannica / USCCB summaries, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Nostra Aetate (1965) repudiated collective Jewish guilt for Christ's death and condemned antisemitism while affirming what is 'true and holy' in other religions, and Dignitatis Humanae (1965) affirmed a right to religious liberty grounded in human dignity - the latter the document traditionalists found hardest to reconcile with the Syllabus of Errors.
s: Nostra Aetate (1965) and Dignitatis Humanae (1965), primary; Britannica summaries, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The meaning of Vatican II is contested between a 'hermeneutic of rupture' (the Bologna School / Giuseppe Alberigo's History of Vatican II, and O'Malley's language-based discontinuity reading) and the 'hermeneutic of reform in continuity' formulated authoritatively by Benedict XVI in his 22 December 2005 Curia address and later endorsed by Francis.
s: Benedict XVI, Address to the Roman Curia (22 Dec 2005), primary; O'Malley, What Happened at Vatican II; O'Collins, Theological Studies, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Paul VI's encyclical Humanae Vitae (25 July 1968) reaffirmed the prohibition of artificial contraception against his own commission's majority, triggering widespread open dissent among Western theologians, clergy, and laity that broke the practical authority of papal moral teaching over ordinary Catholics' sexual lives.
s: Humanae Vitae (1968), primary; standard postconciliar church-history scholarship, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: From about 1965 Mass attendance in majority-Catholic nations fell roughly four percentage points per decade more than in Protestant countries (cumulating to ~20 points by 2010, per an NBER study), and French priests fell from ~41,000 in the mid-1960s to ~15,000 by 2010 - but whether Vatican II caused this or whether secularization, affluence, and Humanae Vitae did is genuinely contested.
s: Harvard Gazette, 'Data bolsters theory about plunging Catholic Mass attendance' (Sep 2025), reporting an NBER working paper, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre founded the SSPX in 1970 to resist Vatican II's reforms, and on 30 June 1988 consecrated four bishops without papal mandate, which John Paul II declared a schismatic act incurring automatic excommunication; Benedict XVI lifted the four bishops' excommunications in 2009 but the SSPX's canonical status remained irregular.
s: Britannica, 'Society of St. Pius X'; Marcel Lefebvre reference accounts; NCRegister/CNA, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: As of mid-2026 the SSPX remains canonically irregular and the confrontation has reignited: the SSPX announced episcopal consecrations on 1 July 2026 at Econe without papal mandate, and on 13 May 2026 Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernandez, DDF prefect, warned the act would be 'a schismatic act' carrying automatic excommunication.
s: Catholic World Report, 'Vatican says SSPX faces excommunications for schismatic bishop consecrations' (13 May 2026); NCRegister/CNA, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: John Paul II (1978-2005), the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, is widely credited with a major role in the peaceful fall of communism (backing Solidarity in Poland), consolidated doctrine (1992 Catechism, Veritatis Splendor, closing the women's-ordination debate), and presided as the clerical abuse crisis broke into the open (the 2002 Boston Globe reporting), with a slow and at times defensive response.
s: PBS Frontline, 'John Paul II And The Fall Of Communism'; Taylor & Francis (2023); standard church-history record, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Benedict XVI announced his resignation on 11 February 2013, effective 28 February 2013, becoming the first pope to relinquish the office since Gregory XII in 1415 - nearly six hundred years - citing the decline of his strength with age.
s: Washington Post, 'Pope Benedict XVI resigns, upending 600 years of tradition' (11 Feb 2013); reference account, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Francis (2013-25), the first Latin American and first Jesuit pope, shifted the Church toward the Global South and the poor (Laudato Si' 2015), opened pastoral questions in Amoris Laetitia (2016) amid sharp polarization (the dubia), made the Synod on Synodality (assemblies 2023/2024) his signature project - declaring the Oct 2024 final document part of the ordinary magisterium - and left a mixed abuse legacy (the 2014 Pontifical Commission, 2019 abolition of pontifical secret, Vos Estis, the Feb 2019 summit, but the unfinished Chile case and incomplete episcopal accountability).
s: USCCB (2024); CNN (24 Apr 2025); NCRonline/OSV (2025), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Pope Francis died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, at 7:35 a.m., aged 88, at Casa Santa Marta in the Vatican (cause registered as stroke and irreversible cardiac arrest following an earlier double-pneumonia hospitalization); his death was announced at 9:47 a.m. by Cardinal Kevin Farrell, the Camerlengo.
s: Vatican News, 'Pope Francis has died on Easter Monday aged 88' (21 Apr 2025); Holy See Press Office Bollettino (21 Apr 2025), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: On 8 May 2025, on the fourth ballot, a conclave of 133 cardinal electors elected Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost as Pope Leo XIV - the first U.S.-born pope (Chicago, 14 Sep 1955; also a Peruvian citizen), the first Augustinian pope, and Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops under Francis since Jan 2023; he chose 'Leo' to echo Leo XIII / Rerum Novarum and to signal a social teaching for the age of artificial intelligence.
s: CNN (8 May 2025); USCCB (2025); Britannica, 'Leo XIV'; CBS News (2025), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: As of June 2026 Leo XIV is an active governing pope: he issued the apostolic exhortation Dilexi Te (4 Oct 2025, on love for the poor, begun by Francis) and his first encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (15 May 2026, on AI and human dignity, released on the 135th anniversary of Rerum Novarum), and he governs through the full College of Cardinals via extraordinary consistories (7-8 Jan 2026 and 26-27 June 2026), intending roughly twice-yearly such meetings.
s: Vatican.va, Magnifica Humanitas (15 May 2026) and Extraordinary Consistory address (7 Jan 2026), primary; America Magazine (2026); NCRegister/CNA (2026), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Survivor-advocacy commentary in mid-2026 frames Leo XIV's 'synodality, Leo-style' as promising but argues the clerical-abuse crisis - Francis's unfinished business - is the real measure of his pontificate, with structural episcopal accountability not yet secured.
s: SNAP, 'Synodality Leo-style holds promise: The clerical abuse crisis is the real test' (21 Jun 2026), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Per the 2025 Annuario Pontificio / 2023 Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae, there were about 1.406 billion Catholics; Africa (~281 million, ~20%) grew ~3.3% with priests rising ~2.7%, the Americas hold ~47.8%, Asia ~11%, while Europe's share and priest numbers declined (priests -1.6%) - a Global-South demographic shift against a still-Rome-centralized institution.
s: Vatican News, 'New data from Annuario Pontificio 2026 shows Catholics growing in Africa' (Mar 2026); Exaudi; The Pillar (Luke Coppen), accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: The twentieth-century ressourcement / nouvelle theologie movement (Henri de Lubac, Yves Congar, Jean Danielou, Hans Urs von Balthasar), a 'return to the sources' of Scripture, the Fathers, and the liturgy that had worked under suspicion of Modernism, supplied the periti and the theological engine of Vatican II - several of its figures later made cardinals by John Paul II.
s: MDPI Religions 10(11):594; Mettepenningen, Nouvelle Theologie (review); Boersma, accessed 25 Jun 2026

claims.t: Catholicism holds Scripture and Tradition to be not two sources but two modes of one deposit of revelation 'flowing from the same divine wellspring' and forming 'one sacred deposit of the word of God' (Dei Verbum 9-10).
s: Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965), paras. 9-10, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Dei Verbum 10 states the teaching office 'is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on' — directly contradicting the popular caricature that the magisterium can teach whatever it likes.
s: Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965), para. 10, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Newman's 1845 Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine articulates doctrine as organic growth ('to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often') and proposes seven non-conclusive 'notes' to distinguish authentic development from corruption; the same Essay is now invoked by both progressives and traditionalists for opposite conclusions.
s: John Henry Newman, An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845), Ch. 1 and Ch. 5, newmanreader.org, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Catholic doctrine is graded into de fide credenda (revealed, requiring the assent of faith), de fide tenenda (definitively held, requiring firm assent), and authentic non-definitive teaching (requiring religious submission of intellect and will, obsequium religiosum), per Ad Tuendam Fidem (1998) and Canons 749-752.
s: John Paul II, Ad Tuendam Fidem (1998) with CDF doctrinal commentary; Code of Canon Law (1983) Cann. 749-752, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Canon 749 §3 of the 1983 Code states that 'no doctrine is understood as defined infallibly unless this is manifestly evident' — a limiting rule routinely omitted from popular accounts and central to disputes over whether teachings like Ordinatio Sacerdotalis or Humanae Vitae are infallible.
s: Code of Canon Law (1983), Canon 749 §3, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Lumen Gentium places Chapter II 'The People of God' before Chapter III on the hierarchy, deliberately reversing the pre-conciliar top-down model and grounding a shared baptismal dignity prior to distinctions of office.
s: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (1964), chapter structure, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Lumen Gentium 8 says the Church of Christ 'subsists in' (subsistit in) the Catholic Church — the drafters changed 'is' (est) to 'subsists in' — and the Vatican's own authoritative interpretation (Dominus Iesus 2000; CDF 2007) reads the change as affirming both that the Church of Christ subsists fully and only in the Catholic Church and that real ecclesial elements exist beyond her.
s: Lumen Gentium (1964) para. 8; CDF, Dominus Iesus (2000) and Responses on the Doctrine on the Church (2007), vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Lumen Gentium 14 restricts the hard form of 'no salvation outside the Church' to those who, knowing the Catholic Church was made necessary by Christ, refuse to enter or remain in it — the conditions 'knowing' and 'refusing' doing the limiting work; LG 16 holds salvation open to the invincibly ignorant.
s: Lumen Gentium (1964), paras. 14 and 16, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Council of Trent (Seventh Session, 1547, Canon 1) defined as dogma that there are exactly seven sacraments instituted by Christ — Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Order, and Matrimony — anathematizing any other count.
s: Council of Trent, Seventh Session (1547), Decree on the Sacraments, Canon 1, EWTN library / papalencyclicals.net, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Trent (Session 7, Canon 8) defined that sacraments confer grace ex opere operato — by the sacramental action itself, not by the minister's holiness or faith alone — a principle that locates the source of grace in Christ acting through the rite, not (as popularly caricatured) a guarantee of grace regardless of the recipient's disposition.
s: Council of Trent, Seventh Session (1547), Canon 8, EWTN library, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Catechism (paras. 1376-1377), quoting Trent, defines transubstantiation as a 'change of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ' (and the wine into his blood), with Christ present 'whole and entire in each of the species'; the term names the fact of the change, not an Aristotelian mechanism the faithful are bound to.
s: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paras. 1376-1377, quoting Council of Trent Session 13, vatican.va / usccb.org, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Penance's matter is the penitent's acts (contrition, confession, satisfaction) and its form the priest's absolution, with perfect contrition (from love of God) distinguished from imperfect (from fear); Holy Orders is conferred in three degrees (bishop with the fullness, priest, deacon) by laying on of hands, with the priest/bishop acting in persona Christi Capitis.
s: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paras. 1422-1470 (Penance) and 1536-1600 (Orders); Council of Trent on Penance, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Trent's Decree on Justification (Session 6, 1547) does not condemn justification by faith but a specific construal: Canon 9 anathematizes 'faith alone' construed as requiring no cooperation or preparation of the will, and Canon 12 condemns reducing justifying faith to mere confidence; Chapter 7 teaches the formal cause is an infused justice 'whereby He maketh us just' (made righteous, not merely declared).
s: Council of Trent, Sixth Session (1547), Decree on Justification, Ch. 7 and Canons 9, 12, 24, 30, papalencyclicals.net / EWTN, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: On 31 October 1999 in Augsburg the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, declaring a consensus on the 'basic truths' ('by grace alone, in faith') such that the 16th-century mutual condemnations no longer apply to the partner's position as now articulated — achieved by 'differentiated consensus' that preserves remaining differences as differences of emphasis, without retracting Trent's canons.
s: LWF & Catholic Church, Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), with Official Common Statement and Annex, lutheranworld.org, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The four defined Marian dogmas are the Divine Motherhood/Theotokos (Ephesus 431), Perpetual Virginity (affirmed Constantinople II 553), the Immaculate Conception (Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 8 Dec 1854), and the Assumption (Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus, 1 Nov 1950) — the Assumption being the clearest undisputed ex cathedra exercise of papal infallibility since 1870.
s: Council of Ephesus (431); Constantinople II (553); Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854); Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus (1950).

claims.t: Catholic moral theology defines natural law (Catechism 1954-1955, quoting Aquinas, ST I-II q.91 a.2) as 'the rational creature's participation of the eternal law,' grounding the claim that moral truth is objective and accessible to reason; Veritatis Splendor (1993) defends the existence of intrinsically evil acts against proportionalism.
s: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paras. 1954-1955; John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor (1993), vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Paul VI's Humanae Vitae (1968) reaffirmed the prohibition of artificial contraception, calling it 'intrinsically wrong' on the principle that 'every conjugal act must remain open to the transmission of life'; whether its central teaching is merely authentic (reformable) or infallible by the ordinary universal magisterium is genuinely contested among Catholic theologians, and it is widely non-observed in the developed-world Church.
s: Paul VI, Humanae Vitae (1968), paras. 11-14, vatican.va; NPR (2018-07-03), accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Catechism defines a double judgment (particular at death, CCC 1022; general/Last at the resurrection), heaven as the beatific vision, purgatory as 'the final purification of the elect' (1031), and hell (1033) primarily as 'definitive self-exclusion from communion with God,' not chiefly as externally imposed punishment; the Church affirms hell's reality but has never defined any particular person is in hell.
s: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paras. 1020-1050, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: On Matthew 16:18-19, modern scholarship (including the Lutheran Oscar Cullmann) largely grants that the 'rock' is Peter himself rather than merely his confession — but notes the text says nothing about succession to the bishops of Rome; the 'keys' evoke the royal-steward office of Isaiah 22:22, a delegated authority. The leap from Petrine to papal primacy is a traditional development, not stated in the text.
s: O. Cullmann, Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr; Brown, Donfried & Reumann (eds.), Peter in the New Testament (1973); exegetical surveys (The Gospel Coalition; Vatican Files), accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Vatican I's Pastor Aeternus (1870) defined two dogmas: the pope's primacy of jurisdiction (ch. 3, 'ordinary and immediate' power over the whole Church) and papal infallibility (ch. 4), the latter restricted by four explicit ex cathedra conditions and declared 'irreformable of themselves, and not by the consent of the church' (against Gallicanism); the jurisdictional dogma is the more consequential and less discussed of the two.
s: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (1870), chs. 3-4, papalencyclicals.net; Vatican News (2020), accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Catechism of the Catholic Church (promulgated by Fidei Depositum, 11 Oct 1992; Latin editio typica 15 Aug 1997; drafted by a Ratzinger-chaired commission incorporating 24,000+ episcopal amendments) is a 'sure norm for teaching the faith' and a reference compendium — not itself a new act of the magisterium defining doctrine; the authority of any paragraph derives from its underlying source, which is why it can be (and in 2018 was, on capital punishment) revised.
s: John Paul II, Fidei Depositum (1992) and Laetamur Magnopere (1997), vatican.va; CCC para. 2267 (2018 revision), accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The 1983 Code of Canon Law (promulgated 25 Jan 1983) has seven books and is theologically ordered by Vatican II: Book II is titled 'The People of God,' its first canon on the faithful (Canon 204) defines all the baptized as Christifideles before distinguishing clergy from laity, and the Code ends (Canon 1752) with 'the salvation of souls must always be the supreme law.
s: Code of Canon Law (1983), Books I-VII; Cann. 204, 749-752, 1752, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pope Leo XIV (elected May 2025) is the reigning pope, and his first encyclical Magnifica Humanitas — signed 15 May 2026, released 25 May 2026 — extends Catholic social teaching to artificial intelligence and human dignity, situated in the tradition from Rerum Novarum through Centesimus Annus and Laudato Si'; its presentation reportedly involved an Anthropic co-founder.
s: Vatican News, 'Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical Magnifica Humanitas' (May 2026); Leo XIV, Magnifica Humanitas (2026), vatican.va; National Catholic Register, full-text report, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The 2021-2024 Synod on Synodality's final document was approved by Francis on 26 October 2024 as participating in 'the ordinary magisterium of the successor of Peter,' with an implementation phase running June 2025 through December 2026; Leo XIV has continued the process (new study groups from July 2025) while the final document preserved the bishop's and pope's decision-taking authority as 'inviolable.
s: Catholic News Agency / EWTN Vatican (Nov 2024); General Secretariat of the Synod, 'Pathways for the Implementation Phase' (Jan 2025); Vatican News (Nov 2025), accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Karl Rahner's 'anonymous Christian' thesis (those who accept God's grace in conscience without explicit faith are saved by Christ though they do not name him) was attacked by Hans Urs von Balthasar in Cordula oder der Ernstfall (1966) for relativizing explicit faith, lacking a theology of the cross, and reducing Christianity to virtuous action; the Church has canonized neither position, leaving inclusivism a genuinely contested question inside the defined boundary.
s: K. Rahner, Theological Investigations (anonymous Christian); H. U. von Balthasar, Cordula oder der Ernstfall (1966); theology-of-religions survey literature, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae 2023 (presented March 2025) counted approximately 1.406 billion baptized Catholics worldwide at end-2023, up 1.15% from ~1.39 billion in 2022.
s: Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae 2023 via Vatican News and Exaudi (March 2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Robert Francis Prevost, an American Augustinian and former Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops, was elected the 267th pope on 8 May 2025 on the fourth ballot, taking the name Leo XIV — the first US-born pope.
s: USCCB and CNN, 8 May 2025; Vatican News, May 2025, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The 2025 conclave was the largest in history; of 135 eligible cardinal electors (under 80 at sede vacante), 133 attended and voted — the first conclave ever to exceed the 120-elector ceiling set by Paul VI.
s: Vatican News (April-May 2025); 2025 conclave coverage, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Roman Curia operates under Francis's apostolic constitution Praedicate Evangelium (19 March 2022, in force 5 June 2022), which reorganized it into 16 dicasteries of equal juridical standing, placed Evangelization first in precedence, and opened the leadership of curial bodies to lay men and women.
s: Praedicate Evangelium (vatican.va, 19 Mar 2022); America Magazine and Catholic World Report, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Sister Simona Brambilla (Consolata Missionaries) was named Prefect of the Dicastery for Institutes of Consecrated Life on 6 January 2025 — the first woman ever to head a Vatican dicastery; the dicastery oversees ~700,000 consecrated persons.
s: Vatican News and America Magazine, 6 January 2025, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Pope Leo XIV appointed lay woman María Montserrat ('Montse') Alvarado (b. 1986, president/COO of EWTN News) as Prefect of the Dicastery for Communication on 2 June 2026, effective 1 November 2026 — the first lay woman to be named a dicastery prefect, succeeding lay prefect Paolo Ruffini.
s: Vatican News and America Magazine, 2 June 2026, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Cardinal Pietro Parolin, Secretary of State since 2013, was retained in post through Leo XIV's first-year curial reshuffle (2026).
s: NCRegister/EWTN Vatican and Aleteia, 2026, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Leo XIV has not reconstituted Francis's Council of Cardinals; it remains nominally listed but has no members, and he instead convenes the whole College, intending an annual multi-day consistory.
s: Catholic Culture, 'What the June consistory reveals about Pope Leo's style of governance,' 2026, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Leo XIV's first extraordinary consistory met 7-8 January 2026, drawing 170 of the then-245 College members, structured in linguistic working groups on synodality, evangelization, curial governance, and liturgy — with no cardinals created.
s: NCRegister and Vatican.va papal address, 7 January 2026, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: As of mid-2026 Leo XIV had created no new cardinals, because Francis left the College above the 120-elector ceiling; both 2026 consistories were consultative, not creating.
s: America Magazine (6 Jan 2026) and NCRegister/Angelus June 2026 previews, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: As of 16 June 2026, the College stood at roughly 241 cardinals, of whom ~117 were electors (under 80) — below the 120 ceiling, as seven cardinals reached 80 during 2026 and Leo created none.
s: Wikipedia 'College of Cardinals' (16 June 2026), cross-checked vs. The Pillar and Catholic-Hierarchy, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Of the 135 cardinal electors eligible in 2025, about 108 (~80%) had been created by Francis; electors came from 70+ countries with ~48% from the Global South, making it the least Eurocentric conclave in history.
s: NPR (April 2025), America Magazine, Vatican News conclave coverage, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: At end-2023 there were 5,430 Catholic bishops (4,258 diocesan, 1,172 from religious orders) governing within 3,041 ecclesiastical jurisdictions, up from 5,353 in 2022, with sharpest growth in Africa and Asia.
s: Annuarium 2023 via EWTN Vatican and Catholic-Hierarchy, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The major men's institutes are in decline — Jesuits ~13,768 (down from ~36,000 in 1965), Salesians ~13,694 (positioned to overtake the Jesuits as the largest), Franciscans OFM ~15,130, Capuchins ~11,092, Benedictines ~7,558; religious sisters fell to 589,423 in 2023 (−9,805 in a year, driven by Europe and the Americas).
s: gcatholic.org and Catholic Culture (2024-2025); America Magazine on Annuarium 2023, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Permanent deacons — ordained ministers who may be married — grew to 51,433 in 2023 and continue rising, concentrated in the Americas and Europe; the one clerical category expanding in the West.
s: America Magazine, 'Vatican stats…,' October 2024 (relaying Annuarium), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Latin Church is governed by the 1983 Code of Canon Law (promulgated 25 Jan 1983 by John Paul II, in force 27 Nov 1983); the 23 Eastern Catholic churches by the parallel Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (CCEO, promulgated 18 Oct 1990, in force 1 Oct 1991).
s: 1983 CIC and 1990 CCEO (primary); USCCB canon-law page, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: As of January 2025 the Holy See held full diplomatic relations with 184 states, operated ~128 nunciatures with 93 resident embassies in Rome, and has been a UN Permanent Observer State since 6 April 1964.
s: Holy See Press Office note via Aleteia (Jan 2026); holyseemission.org, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Provisional Agreement between the Holy See and China on the appointment of bishops (first signed 2018) was renewed for four years on 22 October 2024; Leo XIV has continued the policy, approving appointments under it through 2025.
s: Holy See Press Office communiqué (22 Oct 2024); Detroit Catholic/Crux (2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Holy See reported a 2024 operating deficit of €44.4 million (down from €83.5m in 2023, largely via volatile donations), against a ~€1.2bn budget, while carrying an unaddressed pension liability estimated at €1.5 billion or more.
s: Crux (Nov 2025) and The Pillar; Fortune and Al Jazeera (May 2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR, the 'Vatican Bank') reported a 2024 net profit of €32.8 million (up ~7% from €30.6m in 2023); ASIF recorded a roughly one-third drop in suspicious-activity reports in 2024.
s: FSSPX News and The Pillar (2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: In December 2023 the Vatican tribunal convicted Cardinal Angelo Becciu and others over a London property deal (court-assessed loss ≥€139m), sentencing Becciu to 5 years 6 months; on appeal in March 2026 the court declared a partial mistrial citing prosecutorial procedural errors.
s: CNA (Dec 2023); NCR and OSV News (March 2026), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: At end-2023 Catholics were distributed ~47.8% in the Americas, ~20% in Africa (the fastest-growing region at +3.31%/yr, ~281m), ~20.4% in Europe (stagnant, +0.2%), and ~11% in Asia — a center of gravity sliding toward the Global South.
s: Annuarium 2023 via Vatican News, Exaudi, LiCAS (March 2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: There were 406,996 priests worldwide at end-2023 (−734, −0.2%), declining in Europe (−1.6%) and the Americas (−0.7%) but growing in Africa (+2.7%) and Asia (+1.6%); seminarians fell to 106,495 (−1.8%, the 12th straight year of decline), with Africa the only continent still growing its pipeline (+1.1%).
s: Annuarium 2023 via CatholicVote, Catholic Culture, Vatican News (2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: CARA data show US weekly Mass attendance recovered to ~24% (mid-2023 to early 2025), level with the pre-pandemic 24.4% of 2019 (it had fallen to ~15% in 2020-2023); by contrast ~94% of self-identified Nigerian Catholics attend weekly or daily — the inverse of the Western pattern.
s: CARA via NCR/CNA (2024-2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Pew Research's June 2025 'How the Global Religious Landscape Changed' report found sub-Saharan Africa (31% of all Christians) has overtaken Europe (22%) as the center of Christianity, driven by African birthrates and Western disaffiliation; US Catholicism shows among the steepest net losses of any tradition.
s: Pew Research Center, 9 June 2025; via Angelus and OSV News, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The Catholics-per-priest ratio (pastoral burden) was a Vatican-reported ~3,373 worldwide in 2021 and is rising; it is heaviest where the Church grows fastest (~5,534 in the Americas, ~5,101 in Africa) and lowest in declining Europe (~1,784) — priests are scarcest where the people are most numerous.
s: Annuarium data via Abouna and Exaudi, accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: Leo XIV's first apostolic exhortation, Dilexi te ('I have loved you'), on love for the poor, was signed 4 October 2025 and released 9 October 2025; it completes a project Francis began before his death and runs to ~121 paragraphs across four to five chapters.
s: Dilexi te (vatican.va, 4 Oct 2025); Vatican News (Oct 2025), accessed 2026-06-25

claims.t: The John Jay College report (2004) found allegations against 4,392 U.S. priests for 1950–2002, roughly 4% of the ~109,694 clergy active in the period, with 10,667 individuals making allegations.
s: John Jay College, Nature and Scope of Sexual Abuse of Minors by Catholic Priests 1950–2002 (2004), USCCB; via loc.gov, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: France's CIASE (Sauvé) report, Oct. 5, 2021, estimated ~216,000 children abused by clergy/religious for 1950–2020, rising to ~330,000 including lay Church workers, with 2,900–3,200 abusers — a contested statistical extrapolation, not a verified count.
s: CNA, '330,000 children abused…' Oct. 5, 2021; 'authors respond to critics,' Feb. 10, 2022, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Inquiries outside the US confirmed the abuse pattern: Germany's MHG study (2018) found 3,677 victims / 4.4% of clergy reviewed; Ireland's Ryan and Murphy reports (2009) found endemic abuse and obsessive concealment; Australia's Royal Commission (2017 data) found ~7% of priests alleged perpetrators.
s: NPR Sept. 25, 2018; France24 Sept. 12, 2018; Al Jazeera Oct. 5, 2021, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Boston Globe Spotlight series (first report Jan. 6, 2002) exposed systematic cover-up in the Boston archdiocese via court-released documents; Cardinal Bernard Law resigned Dec. 13, 2002.
s: Boston Globe Spotlight series 2002; Britannica; CBS Boston, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Theodore McCarrick was credibly accused of abuse in June 2018 and laicized Feb. 2019; the Vatican's McCarrick Report (Nov. 10, 2020) documented institutional knowledge enabling his rise — making 'McCarrick' shorthand for the bishop-accountability problem.
s: Vatican McCarrick Report, Nov. 10, 2020; Washington Post Nov. 16, 2020, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The 2018 Pennsylvania grand-jury report detailed credible allegations against 301 priests affecting more than 1,000 identifiable child victims across six dioceses.
s: PBS NewsHour, 'How a Catholic sex abuse report in Pennsylvania echoed around the U.S.,' 2018, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Vos Estis Lux Mundi (motu proprio, May 9, 2019; made permanent April 30, 2023) established universal abuse-reporting and bishop-accountability procedures (the Metropolitan model), extended in 2023 to lay leaders of international associations; critics note bishop-investigations stay bishop-conducted and rarely published.
s: Francis, Vos Estis Lux Mundi, 2019/2023, vatican.va; Catholic World Report, March 25, 2023, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pope Francis convened the Meeting on the Protection of Minors in the Church (Feb. 21–24, 2019), ~190 participants including 114 bishops'-conference presidents; survivor groups judged it insufficient while defenders called it a necessary culture-change.
s: Chicago Catholic, NCRegister, America, NCReporter, Feb–March 2019, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: As of Oct. 31, 2025, Alexandria, LA became the 41st U.S. diocese to file Chapter 11 under abuse-claim pressure; recent settlements include LA ~$880M (Oct 2024), Rockville Centre ~$323M (Dec 2024), Rochester $246.35M (Sept 2025); U.S. dioceses have paid ~$4.4B since 2004, >$5B including religious orders.
s: NCReporter (Alexandria, Oct 2025); NPR Oct. 17, 2024; Rochester Beacon Sept. 8, 2025, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Synod on Synodality (2021–2024) concluded Oct. 27, 2024; Francis directly ratified the Final Document Oct. 26, 2024 — declining the customary exhortation and declaring it part of the 'ordinary magisterium of the Successor of Peter' to be accepted.
s: USCCB 2024; America Nov. 25, 2024; NCRegister Oct. 26, 2024, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pope Leo XIV (Robert Francis Prevost, b. Sept. 14, 1955, Chicago; Augustinian; longtime missionary in Peru) was elected May 8, 2025 on the fourth ballot, becoming the first U.S.-born pope; he signaled continuity with Francis including on synodality.
s: Vatican News biography, May 2025; USCCB 'Pope Leo XIV: A timeline of his first year,' 2026, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pope Leo XIV's June 26–27, 2026 extraordinary consistory took up the next phase of the Synod on Synodality, the international situation, a possible updating of just-war doctrine, and his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas; liturgy was absent from the agenda.
s: Vatican News schedule, June 2026; America June 23, 2026; NCRegister June 2026, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Francis's Traditionis Custodes (July 16, 2021) declared the post-Vatican II books 'the unique expression of the lex orandi of the Roman Rite,' abolishing Benedict's two-forms framework and returning authority over the 1962 Missal to diocesan bishops under Apostolic See guidelines.
s: Francis, Traditionis Custodes, July 16, 2021, vatican.va, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pope Leo XIV has not repealed Traditionis Custodes but signaled de-escalation: he permitted Cardinal Burke to celebrate the traditional Mass at St. Peter's (Sept. 2025) and, in a March 24, 2026 letter to French bishops, called for 'concrete solutions enabling the generous inclusion of those sincerely attached to the Vetus Ordo'; a Roche briefing defending the restrictions was circulated at the Jan. 2026 consistory.
s: America Mar. 26, 2026; NCReporter, 'Defense of Latin Mass restrictions… consistory,' Jan. 2026, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Fiducia Supplicans (DDF, Dec. 18, 2023) authorized non-liturgical blessings of same-sex couples while claiming to change no doctrine; SECAM, on behalf of Africa's bishops and with Francis's agreement, declared in January 2024 that such blessings 'cannot be carried out in Africa without exposing themselves to scandals' — the largest collective rejection of a Francis-era document.
s: America Jan. 11, 2024; SECAM statement Jan. 2024; Vatican News Jan. 2024, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: As of mid-2026 Fiducia Supplicans remains in force, applied unevenly by geography (parts of the West vs. effectively a dead letter in Africa); Pope Leo XIV has made no move to repeal or expand it — a status partly inferred from the absence of any contrary act.
s: EWTN Vatican, 'Global Responses to Fiducia Supplicans a Year Later,' 2024, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: John Paul II's Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (May 22, 1994) declared the Church 'has no authority whatsoever' to ordain women priests, 'to be definitively held'; the 1995 CDF responsum (approved by JPII) said the teaching was 'set forth infallibly by the ordinary and universal Magisterium' — a note that women's-ordination advocates contest.
s: John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, May 22, 1994, vatican.va; CDF Responsum, Oct. 1995, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Francis created study commissions on the women's diaconate (2016 and 2020); under Leo XIV, a Dec. 4, 2025 letter from Cardinal Petrocchi summarized commission votes (e.g., seven members favored that the ancient female diaconate lacked sacramental character) without a formal decision, and Study Group 5's March 10, 2026 report did not address women deacons directly, recommending 'new ministries' instead; the question formally 'remains open.
s: America, 'Where the women deacons question stands at the Vatican,' Mar. 13, 2026, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: In Querida Amazonia (Feb. 2, 2020) Francis declined to act on the Amazon Synod's recommendation to ordain married men (viri probati), neither approving nor formally closing the door — the template for governance by non-decision; no general or regional celibacy change exists as of mid-2026.
s: CNA Feb. 2020; America Feb. 12, 2020, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The German Synodal Way's successor body, a 'Synodal Conference' of 27 diocesan bishops and 27 ZdK lay representatives with equal voting rights, had its statutes approved by the ZdK (late 2025) and adopted by the German Bishops' Conference plenary on Feb. 24, 2026; the statutes were submitted to Rome for recognitio ad experimentum, with Vatican approval not granted as of early 2026.
s: The Pillar 2025/2026; Catholic Herald Feb. 2026; INFOVATICANA Feb. 25, 2026, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The German Synodal Way is the most acute schism risk in the Church as of mid-2026: Rome warned a permanent synodal council would place itself 'above' the bishops' conference; Cardinal Woelki declared in January 2026 'For me the Synodal Way is concluded'; and Bishop Bätzing, the Way's chief episcopal champion, announced Jan. 19, 2026 he would not seek reelection as DBK president.
s: Catholic World Report, Jan. 27, 2026; The Pillar/Catholic Herald, Jan–Feb 2026, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The secret Vatican–China Provisional Agreement on bishop appointments (first signed Sept. 22, 2018) was renewed for the first time for a four-year term in October 2024 (its third renewal); about ten bishops have been appointed under it since 2018, and it remains in force as of mid-2026.
s: Vatican News Oct. 22, 2024; NBC News Oct. 2024, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Critics led by Cardinal Joseph Zen call the China deal a betrayal that hands Beijing veto power; Beijing has unilaterally appointed/transferred bishops (2022, 2023) without Vatican veto; Human Rights Watch urged a review (May 12, 2025); and Leo XIV continued the deal, appointing a Chinese bishop under its framework in June 2025.
s: NBC News Oct. 2024; HRW May 12, 2025; International Christian Concern June 12, 2025, accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Catholic media is bifurcated in a way scholars compare to U.S. political polarization: EWTN (Irondale, AL) owns the National Catholic Register and Catholic News Agency on the conservative side, while the National Catholic Reporter (progressive), America (Jesuit), and Commonweal anchor the other — with the near-identical Reporter/Register names being opposite in lean.
s: National Catholic Reporter, 'From the Bible Belt, EWTN shapes world Catholic news,' accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy share apostolic succession, seven sacraments, a real-presence sacrificial Eucharist, devotion to Mary and the saints, monasticism, and the rejection of sola scriptura — making them two branches of one sacramental-episcopal tree rather than two religions.
s: Balamand Document, Joint International Commission for Theological Dialogue, 23 June 1993, christianunity.va, para. 13; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The decisive Catholic-Orthodox divergence is structural: Rome's centralized magisterium with a pope holding ordinary, immediate, universal jurisdiction and the power to teach infallibly (Vatican I, 1870) versus Orthodoxy's communion of autocephalous churches with no single visible head — the 'road not taken.
s: Ravenna Document, Joint International Commission, 13 Oct 2007; First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, 1870; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Western insertion of 'filioque' ('and the Son') into the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed is both a Trinitarian dispute and a jurisdictional one — the East holds no local church may unilaterally alter an ecumenical creed — crystallizing in the Photian controversy (9th c.) and the repudiated Florence union (1439).
s: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli, 1439; history of the filioque controversy (substantive claims traced to conciliar texts); accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pope Leo XIV traveled to Türkiye for the 1,700th anniversary of Nicaea and signed a joint declaration with Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I in Istanbul on 29 November 2025, pledging to continue toward 'full communion between our sister Churches,' rejecting 'absorption or domination,' and proposing a common Easter date.
s: Joint Declaration of Leo XIV and Bartholomew I, Istanbul, 29 Nov 2025, vatican.va; Vatican News 2025-11; America Magazine 2025-11-28; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Vatican II reframed the Orthodox as 'sister churches' with true sacraments and apostolic succession, and in 1965 Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras mutually lifted the 1054 excommunications — a 'healing of memory' that changed atmosphere without resolving substance.
s: Balamand Document para. 14, 1993; Catholic-Eastern Orthodox relations historiography; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Orthodoxy lacks a single negotiating partner: the Moscow delegation walked out of Ravenna (2007) over Estonian representation, and Moscow broke communion with Constantinople in 2018 over Ukrainian autocephaly — exposing the absence of a supreme arbiter in the autocephalous model and limiting ecumenical progress.
s: Ravenna Document context and reporting, 2007; Catholic-Eastern Orthodox relations coverage; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: On 31 October 1999 in Augsburg, the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, declaring 'a consensus in basic truths' — that 'by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work...we are accepted by God' — via 'differentiated consensus' that left language differences real but not church-dividing.
s: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, LWF/Catholic Church, 31 Oct 1999; Official Common Statement JD 40-41, lutheranworld.org / christianunity.va; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The deepest, least-negotiable Catholic-Protestant divide is authority: Catholicism's Scripture-plus-Tradition interpreted by a living magisterium versus the Reformation's sola scriptura — the issue the JDDJ did not touch and the reason its justification agreement left the relationship fundamentally unchanged.
s: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, 1999 (scope); Catholic ecclesiology on the magisterium; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: A Pew Research Center study released 21 January 2026 (spring 2024 survey, 6,200+ adults, six countries) found Catholic shares down 9+ points in every country since 2013-14: Argentina 71%→58%, Brazil and Chile to 46%, Colombia down 19 points to 60%, Mexico to 67%, Peru steady at 67%.
s: Pew Research Center, 'Catholicism Has Declined in Latin America Over the Past Decade,' 21 Jan 2026, pewresearch.org; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Former Catholics' destinations differ by country: Brazil leaks mainly to Protestantism (29% Protestant; 13% raised-Catholic-now-Protestant), while Mexico, Argentina, Chile, and Colombia leak mainly to disaffiliation (Mexico: 15% raised-Catholic-now-none vs. 4% now-Protestant); 'nones' roughly doubled to quadrupled across the six countries.
s: Pew Research Center, 'Religious identity and switching in Latin American countries,' 21 Jan 2026, pewresearch.org; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: In Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, evangelicals (overwhelmingly Pentecostal) now rival or outnumber Catholics — Guatemala ~45% Catholic vs. ~42% Protestant in the mid-2010s with evangelical plurality projected by ~2030 — inverting a region that was Catholic by supermajority within living memory.
s: Sight Magazine, 'Evangelicals now outnumber Catholics in three Central American nations'; Pew, 'Historical Overview of Pentecostalism in Guatemala,' 2006; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae 2023 (released March 2025) records global Catholics at 1.406 billion (2023), with Africa the fastest-growing region (+3.31% in a year, to 281 million; DR Congo ~55 million), and ~406,996 priests worldwide, with priest numbers rising in Africa/Asia and falling in Europe (-1.6%).
s: Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae 2023 / Annuario Pontificio 2025, Central Office for Church Statistics, via EWTN Vatican & Catholic World Report, March 2025; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pentecostalism wins converts the parish loses via four mechanisms — lay leadership/low ordination barriers, healing and prosperity emphasis, intensity of community, and expressive worship — analyzed by David Martin (free social space, socioeconomic mobility) and R. Andrew Chesnut (religious-economy 'marketplace,' healing as 'product,' women as principal market).
s: David Martin, Tongues of Fire (Blackwell 1990); R. Andrew Chesnut, Competitive Spirits (OUP 2003); consulted via scholarly summaries; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity grew from fewer than one million adherents in 1900 to a movement projected to exceed one billion by 2050 — the single most consequential structural fact about Christianity's recent shape.
s: Zurlo, Johnson & Crossing, World Christianity 2025, CSGC/Gordon-Conwell, via accessible CSGC-derived reporting; accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: The Catholic Church is a communion of 24 churches sui iuris — the Latin Church plus 23 Eastern Catholic churches across five ritual families — the largest being the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church (~5.5 million, Byzantine) and the Syro-Malabar Church of Kerala (~4.5 million, East Syriac), governed under a separate Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990).
s: Annuario Pontificio 2023 via Catholic News Agency & Catholics & Cultures (Boston College); accessed 2026-06-25.

claims.t: In June 2014, under Pope Francis, the Congregation for the Eastern Churches (Cardinal Sandri) rescinded the 1929 decree Cum data fuerit, restoring in universal law the traditional Eastern Catholic practice of ordaining married men to the priesthood in the diaspora (North/South America, Australia).
s: National Catholic Reporter, 'Vatican lifts ban on married priests for Eastern Catholics in diaspora,' 2014; Catholic Culture, 2014; accessed 2026-06-25.
